- **MeshCore's "USB capture sources" card now shows live readouts per companion, matching Serial's layout.** Previously every readout (Node ID/Frequency/Bandwidth/SF/TX Power/Firmware/Hardware) lived in a single separate "MeshCore Companion" card sourced from `_tx_service._meshcore_tx` -- the one companion wired for sending -- so a second or third configured companion showed no readouts of its own at all, and the section sat awkwardly above the channel/chatrooms table. Root cause was architectural, not cosmetic: each `MeshcoreUsbCaptureSource` already holds its own independent connection (`self._meshcore`, used for RSSI/SNR signal extraction) but had no way to surface its own radio/firmware status. Fixed by giving each companion source its own `get_radio_info()`/`get_device_info()` (the parsing logic factored out of `MeshCoreTxClient` into standalone `read_radio_status()`/`read_device_info()` functions so both share it without duplication), a new `_find_meshcore_sources()` (plural) in `server.py`, and a new `GET /api/config` field, `meshcore.companions` (one entry per configured companion, keyed by its `meshcore_usb_<label>` name, mirroring how `serial` already reports one entry per stick). The readouts moved into each companion's own row in the "USB capture sources" card; the separate "MeshCore Companion" card now only holds the editable name/advert controls and the shared channel table, since renames and channel sync still only ever target company[0]. The firmware "Check for updates" button is now per-companion too: `GET /api/config/meshcore/firmware-check` takes a `current_version` query param instead of resolving the primary companion server-side (exactly mirroring Serial's identical fix above), and its cache now stores only the shared GitHub fetch rather than a full comparison result, since multiple companions can be on different firmware simultaneously. TX routing itself (which companion actually sends) is untouched -- still always company[0], out of scope for this fix. **Fixed a regression found live immediately after deploying this**: the per-companion row showed "Not connected" even for a genuinely connected companion (readouts and the Check-for-updates button both vanished). Root cause: `MeshcoreUsbCaptureSource` only ever tracked connection state as a private `self._connected` -- it never had a public `connected` property like `serial_source.py` does -- so `config_routes.py`'s `getattr(src, "connected", False)` found no such attribute and silently defaulted to `False` every time, regardless of the real live state (which the topbar chip and the old single-companion card both read correctly, through a different wrapper object that does expose `connected`). Added the missing `@property def connected(self)` to `MeshcoreUsbCaptureSource`, mirroring Serial's exact pattern.
- **Every MeshCore companion can now be renamed and adverted independently, not just the primary.** User asked, looking at the "Companion name" section: "is this for the first or second companion... maybe we need it in every companion section." Correct catch: the rename card called `MeshCoreTxClient.set_companion_name()`, which -- like TX/status before the readouts fix above -- only ever targets company[0] (the one companion the TX client is bound to via `_find_meshcore_source()`); a second companion couldn't be renamed at all. Fixed the same way as the readouts: `set_companion_name()`/`send_advert()`'s validation and command logic factored out of `MeshCoreTxClient` into standalone `send_set_companion_name()`/`send_companion_advert()` functions (mirroring `read_radio_status()`/`read_device_info()`'s existing pattern), and `MeshcoreUsbCaptureSource` gained its own `set_companion_name()`/`send_advert()` methods calling those against its own connection. The Companion Name field, "Send advert after save" checkbox, and Save button all moved from the shared "MeshCore Companion" card into each companion's own row in "USB capture sources" (that card now only holds connection status and the shared channel table, since MeshCore channel keys are genuinely mesh-wide config, unlike per-device identity). `PUT /api/config/meshcore/companion-name` gained a `label` field to target a specific companion; new `POST /api/config/meshcore/companion-advert` (also label-scoped) replaces the rename flow's advert-after-save call, since the general `POST /api/messages/advert` always hits company[0] regardless of which companion was just renamed. Persistence: `MeshcoreUsbConfig` gained its own per-companion `companion_name` field (`capture.meshcore_usb[i].companion_name`) re-applied on every reconnect for that specific companion (each companion source now gets its own connected-callback, not just the primary) -- the old mesh-wide `meshcore.companion_name` field stays as a fallback for the primary companion only, so existing `local.yaml` files with the old singular field keep working unchanged. Also fixed a latent bug this surfaced: `PUT /api/config/capture/meshcore-companions` (the "Save USB sources" button) replaced the whole companion list from the request body, which has no `companion_name` field at all -- saving that form (e.g. just to add a new companion) would have silently wiped every existing companion's configured name. Now preserves each companion's `companion_name` by label match across that save. Verified: label-resolution (own name vs. legacy-fallback-for-primary-only vs. bare/unlabeled companion, 5 scenarios), the standalone rename/advert functions against a stubbed connection (success/rejected/empty-name/not-connected paths), and the companion-list-save name-preservation fix, all via stubbed fastapi/meshcore (no real deps on Mac); frontend identity block prefill (persisted name / live-name fallback / blank / XSS-escaping) via a DOM stub. `py_compile`d all six touched Python files, `node --check`ed; CHANGELOG/README updated.
- **Topbar now shows one MeshCore chip per companion, matching the Meshtastic USB chips.** User noticed only one MeshCore chip showed in the topbar despite having two companions (868 and 433) configured and live. Root cause: `TopbarMeshcoreChip` (`frontend/topbar/topbar_meshcore_chip.js`) was hardcoded to one static `<span class="topbar-meshcore">` in `index.html` and read only the singular `meshcore.connected`/`meshcore.radio`/`meshcore.companion_name` fields -- it never looked at the `meshcore.companions` array this session's earlier readouts fix already added to `GET /api/config`. `TopbarSerialChip` already solved the identical problem correctly (an empty container div, one badge built per array entry) -- this was a pure frontend port of that exact pattern to MeshCore, no backend changes needed since the per-companion data already existed. Rewrote `TopbarMeshcoreChip` to take a single container element and build one badge per `meshcore.companions` entry (name/lamp/frequency, keyed by the companion's own `meshcore_usb_<label>` name for a short label suffix when set); channel name still comes from the shared `meshcore.channel_keys` since MeshCore channels are genuinely mesh-wide config (same value shown on every badge, not a per-badge stand-in). `index.html`'s `#topbar-meshcore-group` is now an empty container like `#topbar-serial-group`, instead of wrapping one static chip. Verified via a DOM stub: two distinct companion badges built correctly from real-shaped data (869.618 MHz "868" + 433.65 MHz "433"), the group hides with zero companions, and the dashboard-unreachable/reconnecting state renders without throwing. `node --check`ed. **Fixed a live-found styling bug**: user reported both companion chips' lamp dots showed dull grey instead of green, and didn't blink amber while reconnecting. Root cause: the CSS keys the dot's color/blink animation off a *modifier* class on the lamp element itself (`.topbar-meshcore__lamp--online .topbar-meshcore__dot`, `topbar.css:240-257`), not the badge root -- the rewrite above set `lamp.className = 'topbar-meshcore__lamp'` (base class only) and never added the `--online`/`--offline`/`--reconnecting` suffix, a state the old static markup's dedicated `_setLamp()` method used to add but which had no equivalent in the new per-badge `_buildBadge()`. Fixed by building the lamp's className with the state suffix included. Verified via an improved DOM stub (properly clearing children on `textContent = ''`, matching real DOM behavior): all three lamp states now carry their modifier class. **Reordered the topbar groups**: user asked for Meshtastic chips grouped together before MeshCore chips ("now its a mix match") -- `index.html`'s `#topbar-serial-group` (Meshtastic USB sticks) now comes before `#topbar-meshcore-group` (MeshCore companions), so the concentrator's own Meshtastic chip, any Meshtastic USB stick chips, and MeshCore companion chips render in that protocol-grouped order instead of interleaved. Pure DOM reorder -- each chip controller populates its own container independently of position, no JS or CSS ordering rules depend on the previous arrangement.
- **Meshtastic USB serial devices can now be renamed from the dashboard.** User asked whether Serial had the same rename+advert feature MeshCore companions just got, then clarified why it matters: "there the nodes/companion dont have bluetooth only direct serial" -- these sticks can't be renamed via the official Meshtastic app's usual Bluetooth path, so the dashboard is the only practical way. Confirmed via the actually-installed `meshtastic` Python package (found under Homebrew's Python 3.11, not the Mac's default `python3`) rather than guessing: `Node.setOwner(long_name, short_name)` sends an `ADMIN_APP` AdminMessage, the same mechanism `send_nodeinfo()` (already existed) rides on for TX -- but its real source also revealed a genuine hazard: `setOwner()` calls a CLI-oriented `our_exit()` helper (`print()` + `sys.exit(1)`) on an empty or whitespace-only name, which would have killed this entire long-running server process if ever reached. New `SerialCaptureSource.set_owner()` strips and validates both names (36/4-char ceilings, matching the concentrator's own existing Identity route) *before* ever calling the real `setOwner()`, making that path unreachable by construction, plus a defensive `except SystemExit` as a last-resort safety net. `send_nodeinfo()` also fixed to read long/short name from this source's own cache (updated immediately by a successful rename) instead of re-querying `iface.getMyNodeInfo()`, which isn't guaranteed to reflect a local rename right away -- so an advert sent immediately after renaming announces the *new* name, not a stale one. New `PUT /api/config/serial/identity` and `POST /api/config/serial/advert` (both label-scoped, mirroring `meshcore_config_routes.py`'s companion-name/companion-advert shape exactly); `SerialDeviceConfig` gained `long_name`/`short_name` fields (`capture.serial[i]`), applied once at connect (`start()`) since, unlike MeshCore's companions, `SerialCaptureSource` has no auto-reconnect loop to hook a live re-apply into -- a swapped-in replacement stick picks up the configured name on the next service restart instead, matching this card's existing "Requires a service restart after changes" convention. Also fixed the same latent list-save wipe bug found in MeshCore's equivalent: `PUT /api/config/capture/serial-devices` rebuilt every device fresh from the request body (no long/short name fields in that shape at all), so saving the USB sources form would have silently erased configured names -- now preserves them by label match. UI: each device row in "USB capture sources" gains Long name / Short name fields, a "Send advert after save" checkbox, and a Save button (mirrors MeshCore's identity block, `frontend/js/configuration/serial_card.js`). Verified: 9 scenarios for `set_owner()` against a stubbed interface (happy path, empty/overlong names rejected *before* the real call, `None`-for-both passthrough, `SystemExit` caught without escaping, an ordinary radio exception handled, not-connected, and `send_nodeinfo()` preferring the freshly-updated cache over stale library state), label-resolution and list-save preservation logic, and the frontend identity block's prefill/XSS-escaping via a DOM stub. `py_compile`d all seven touched Python files, `node --check`ed. CHANGELOG/README/CONFIGURATION.md updated. **Fixed a live-found hang immediately after deploying this**: user reported the rename status stuck on "Renaming device…" indefinitely. Root cause: this method also called `iface.waitForAckNak()` after `setOwner()`, mirroring `getMetadata()`'s existing pattern -- but `Node.setOwner()`'s own real source sets `onResponse=None` specifically for the local/directly-attached node case (renaming *yourself*, as opposed to a remote mesh node), so nothing ever sets the `receivedAck`/`receivedNak` flags that call is waiting on. `waitForAckNak()` busy-waits with blocking `time.sleep()` (not `asyncio.sleep()`) for its full 20-second default timeout before giving up -- and since this runs synchronously inside an async FastAPI route handler with no executor, it froze the *entire dashboard's event loop* for 20 seconds on every single rename attempt, not just the one request. Fixed by removing the `waitForAckNak()` call entirely: `sendData()` (which `setOwner()` rides on) already queues the write and returns immediately regardless, and the local-node `onResponse=None` design is the library authors' own signal that no ack wait is expected here. Verified via a stub whose fake `waitForAckNak()` now raises if ever called (confirming it's genuinely unreachable) across all 4 previously-passing scenarios.
- **Meshtastic and MeshCore tabs' Recent Packets tables gain a Frequency column, matching the Dashboard's.** User: "since we have 2 freq on each platform" (868+433 Meshtastic via concentrator+USB stick, 868+433 MeshCore via two companions) -- with multiple bands live on both protocols, telling which frequency a given packet came from wasn't possible from either tab's table, only the Dashboard's own combined feed showed it. Turned out to be a pure frontend fix: both `/api/meshcore/packets` and `/api/meshtastic/packets` already returned `frequency_mhz` per packet (same DB column populated from each packet's own `signal.frequency_mhz` at capture time, `packet_repository.py`), just never rendered as a column in `meshcore_panel.js`/`meshtastic_panel.js` -- no backend changes needed. New Freq column (one decimal place, `--` when absent) between SNR and SF, matching the Dashboard's own column order. `col-freq` width rule added to `lorawan.css` for both tables' colgroups.
- **Serial port fields now suggest connected USB devices, and prefer stable paths over `/dev/ttyUSBn`.** User asked for a dropdown of enumerated devices on the "Pinned serial port" field, then recalled an earlier open suggestion in the project notes about pinning by `/dev/serial/by-id/...` instead of raw `ttyUSBn` numbers for robustness. Checked the user's own Pi before building anything, which caught a real problem with the by-id idea: `ls -la /dev/serial/by-id/` showed only 2 symlinks for 3 physical devices -- two Heltec V3 boards share the same unprogrammed factory-default CP2102 serial number (`0001`), so they collide on the same by-id name and one device silently gets no symlink at all. `/dev/serial/by-path/` (keyed on physical USB port, not the device's own serial number) gave all 3 devices distinct entries instead, confirmed against the user's actual `ls -la` output. Built `usb_classifier.py`'s new `list_serial_ports_with_stable_paths()`: enumerates via the same `serial.tools.list_ports.comports()` this module already used for GPS-stick filtering, resolves each device against both `/dev/serial/by-id/` and `/dev/serial/by-path/`, and recommends `by-path > by-id > raw device` as the value to pin -- by-path wins by default specifically because it stays unique even when by-id collides, the exact scenario confirmed on this project's own hardware. New `GET /api/config/serial-ports` (`system_config_routes.py`, read-only, any logged-in session) lists connected devices with their resolved stable path. Frontend: both `meshcore_card.js` and `serial_card.js`'s "Pinned serial port"/"Serial port" fields gained a shared `<datalist>` (native HTML combo-box: pick from what's plugged in right now, or still type a path manually for a device that isn't connected yet), refreshed on every render so newly plugged devices show up without a reload. Trade-off documented in the API docstring and the field's own hint text: by-path ties identity to the physical USB port, not the board -- moving a device to a different port makes it look like a new device rather than following it, but that's still strictly better than raw `ttyUSBn` numbering, which can shift on any reconnect regardless of port. Verified: the exact 3-device collision scenario from the user's own Pi (one device with NO by-id entry, all 3 getting distinct by-path values), the graceful fallback when neither symlink directory exists (Mac dev environment) or pyserial is missing, and the datalist-population logic (including a failed-fetch case that must not throw) via a DOM stub. `py_compile`d, `node --check`ed. **Two follow-on refinements from the same conversation**: (1) the dropdown now also filters out the Pi's own onboard UARTs (`/dev/ttyAMA0`, `/dev/ttyS0`) -- those have no USB VID/PID and were cluttering a picker meant specifically for USB devices, filtered server-side (`vid is not None`) rather than in the frontend. (2) each option's label now includes the underlying `/dev/ttyUSBn` name in parentheses (e.g. "Silicon Labs CP2102 USB to UART Bridge Controller (ttyUSB1)") -- with two identical-looking CP2102 entries in the list, the by-path value alone didn't make it obvious which was which; a new "↻ Rescan USB" button next to "+ Add companion"/"+ Add device" also lets a user unplug/replug a device and see it in the list immediately, without waiting for the next automatic dashboard poll. **Third follow-on**: the picker now warns when a device is already claimed by another configured companion or serial device, cross-checked across BOTH protocols -- not just within the current card -- since MeshCore and Serial pin from the same physical USB pool, and nothing previously stopped accidentally pointing two config slots at the same port. New `_buildPortUsageMap(config)` in both cards maps every currently-configured `serial_port` value (from `capture.meshcore_usb` AND `capture.serial`) to a human label ("MeshCore 868", "Serial 433"), matched against each candidate's raw device/by-id/by-path forms so an older config still pinned by a raw `/dev/ttyUSBn` path is recognized too; a claimed option's label gets an "— already used by ..." suffix. Still selectable (a native `<datalist>` option can't be disabled, and a row showing its own already-pinned port correctly sees this label too -- not a bug). Verified via a DOM stub: cross-protocol matching by raw device path, cross-protocol matching by a by-path value, and a genuinely unused port staying unflagged. **Fourth follow-on, found live**: user reported the "already used" warning text was present but got cut off and unreadable in the browser's native datalist popup, which truncates long labels with no CSS control over wrapping or width -- the warning, appended at the END of a full "Silicon Labs ... USB to UART Bridge Controller" descriptor string, was exactly the part getting cut off. New `_portOptionLabel(p, usage)` (shared logic in both cards) shortens each label dramatically and reorders it so the critical bits come first: `ttyUSB1 — CP2102 — used by MeshCore 868` instead of `Silicon Labs CP2102 USB to UART Bridge Controller (ttyUSB1) — already used by MeshCore 868` -- device name first (for quick disambiguation), then a trimmed chip name (the "Silicon Labs .../USB to UART Bridge Controller" boilerplate is identical and uninformative across every CP210x device anyway), then the usage warning only when applicable. Verified via a DOM stub: both the with-usage and without-usage label formats. **Fifth follow-on**: user asked to also show the resolved `/dev/ttyUSBn` next to the pinned field itself once a device is already selected -- a by-path value like `/dev/serial/by-path/platform-fd500000.pcie-pci-0000:01:00.0-usb-0:1.2:1.0-port0` is not something anyone can eyeball as "which physical ttyUSBn is that." New `_updateResolvedPort(input)` (shared logic in both cards) shows a small `→ /dev/ttyUSB0`-style hint below the field, matched against the enumerated ports' stable_path/by_id/by_path/device forms (so it resolves regardless of which form the pinned value happens to be in) -- updates live on every keystroke/selection (`input` event) and again once the async port enumeration actually arrives (a row can render before that fetch resolves). Clears rather than showing stale info when the pinned value doesn't currently match anything connected, and stays silent when the value is already the raw device path itself (nothing useful to add). New `.cfg-field__resolved` CSS rule (`configuration.css`, `:empty { display: none; }` so it takes no layout space when blank). Verified via 4 scenarios: resolves correctly, clears on no match, no redundant self-arrow when already showing the raw device, and clears on an empty field.
- **install.sh: rtl_433, welle.io, and the Meshtastic/MeshCore CLI tools skip reinstalling if already present.** User: "can you guard them with a check if they already installed like we do on 7 and 8, dont install if already installed?" Sections 7 (redsea) and 8 (multimon-ng) already had this `command -v <binary> || install` guard since they're built from source; sections 9-11 (rtl_433, welle.io, meshtastic/meshcore CLI) installed unconditionally via apt/pip/pipx every single run. Added the same idempotency guard: `rtl_433` (section 9), `welle-cli` (section 10 -- the actual binary Meshpoint's DAB+ tab drives, not the GUI-only `welle.io` binary the same package also installs), and `meshtastic`/`meshcore-cli` (section 11, each guarded independently since two separate tools are installed there). `bash -n`-checked.
- **MeshCore packets stored with the wrong (bare) capture source, silently masking which companion actually captured them.** User spotted a packet's detail modal showing `Source: meshcore_usb` (bare, no `_868`/`_433` suffix) for a today-timestamped, genuinely live-received packet, and initially suspected the shown frequency (433.65 MHz) was wrong for an external node they believed to be on 868 MHz -- traced it down together and confirmed the frequency was actually correct (the packet's own public key didn't match either of the user's own companions' node IDs, confirming it was a genuinely-heard external node on the 433 companion, which physically could not have received an 868 MHz transmission). The real bug: `MeshcoreUsbCaptureSource._wrap_event()` (`src/capture/meshcore_usb_source.py`) hardcoded `capture_source="meshcore_usb"` as a literal string instead of reading `self.name` (which correctly returns `meshcore_usb_868`/`meshcore_usb_433` per the labeled `MeshcoreUsbConfig` entry) -- every packet from either companion, always, landed in the database with the bare source string, discarding the very distinction the multi-companion labeling feature exists to provide. `self.name` is already used correctly everywhere else in the codebase (`server.py`'s source lookups) -- this was the one spot the original multi-companion refactor missed. Confirmed no other code does an exact `== "meshcore_usb"` match against a packet's stored `capture_source` (the only exact matches found compare against `config.capture.sources`, a completely different list of capture-source *types*, not per-packet attribution) -- everything else already uses `.startswith("meshcore_usb")` or filters by protocol instead, so this fix is safe going forward. One-line fix: `capture_source=self.name`. Verified via 3 scenarios: a labeled 433 companion stamps `meshcore_usb_433`, a labeled 868 companion stamps `meshcore_usb_868` (distinct from the 433 one), and a bare/unlabeled single-companion setup still correctly falls back to bare `meshcore_usb`. `py_compile`d. Only affects newly-captured packets going forward -- existing rows already stored with the bare source stay as they are (no backfill).
- **MeshCore node names cross-contaminated between genuinely different physical nodes -- a real, live-found data-integrity bug, not a one-off.** Follow-up to the capture-source fix above: user's own new 433 companion (node_id `c7fa575ac983`, first-seen the same day) showed up in the Nodes list as "PD2EMC UMESH" -- the name of a completely unrelated external node the user knows personally (real key `e71d1ab3b647...`, connected via TCP through Home Assistant). Querying the live database (a copy the user pulled from the Pi) showed this wasn't isolated: **dozens** of long_name values were shared across 2-5 genuinely distinct node_ids project-wide. Root cause, found via Explore subagent tracing every code path that writes `nodes.long_name` for MeshCore rows: `server.py`'s `on_text_packet` handler had a fallback (fired whenever a MeshCore node's name couldn't be resolved normally) that ran `SELECT node_id, long_name FROM nodes WHERE node_id LIKE 'mc:%' ...` with **no WHERE clause tied to the current packet's sender at all** -- it grabbed some arbitrary "mc:"-prefixed roster-placeholder row (SQLite returns whichever one its query planner picks, with no ORDER BY) and stamped that unrelated name onto whichever node actually triggered the fallback. Two sibling bugs of the same shape were found nearby and fixed too: (1) the same handler's two OTHER name-propagation queries matched by an 8-hex-char (32-bit) `LIKE 'prefix%'` guess instead of the node's own full 12-char canonical ID, a real (if lower-probability) collision surface in its own right -- tightened to exact `=` matches; (2) `_refresh_mc_contacts()`'s in-memory name cache indexed every roster contact by FOUR different prefix lengths (8/10/12/16 chars) instead of just the canonical 12, letting two contacts sharing a short prefix silently overwrite each other's cached name -- narrowed to the 12-char form only, matching `node_id`'s own established truncation (`meshcore_event_adapter.py`'s `pubkey[:12]`); (3) `meshcore_contacts.py`'s `sync_meshcore_contacts_to_nodes()` had the identical graduated-prefix-length flaw (`_meshcore_pubkey_prefixes()`, tried 16/12/10/8-char attempts) -- removed the helper entirely, now a single exact 12-char match. All four fixes converge on the same principle: MeshCore node identity is already canonically truncated to 12 hex chars everywhere else in this codebase; matching on anything shorter for a "same node" guess is what caused every one of these bugs. Verified via a stub reproducing the exact production scenario (a brand-new companion with no name yet no longer inherits an unrelated roster contact's cached name; the real contact still resolves correctly to its own name). New `scripts/clear_meshcore_name_contamination.py`: a dry-run-by-default cleanup script for the ALREADY-corrupted data (only these code paths are fixed going forward; existing wrong names needed a separate pass) -- flags a real node's name only when (a) 2+ distinct real node_ids currently share that exact name AND (b) an existing roster placeholder independently carries the same name too (the specific signature of the fixed bug, avoiding false positives on real devices that coincidentally share a generic factory-default name with no roster connection at all, e.g. multiple SenseCap units all broadcasting "SenseCap_Solar Repeater"). Tested dry-run and `--apply` against a real copy of the production database: correctly narrowed from an initial naive over-broad detection (which wrongly flagged 18 nodes, including many single-node false positives) down to exactly the 3 confirmed victims, leaving the legitimate roster placeholder untouched. `py_compile`d all touched files.
- **Stray Frames card on the RF Environment page.** RF frames that don't decode as LoRaWAN, Meshtastic, or MeshCore no longer vanish silently — they're now captured (time, capture source, protocol hint if any, size, RSSI/SNR, raw hex, expandable per row) in a new wide card below the channel histogram. Deliberately an in-memory ring buffer (newest 500, cleared on restart) rather than a database table for now: broadband capture on the SX1302 could plausibly see far more undecodable RF than genuine traffic, and there's no way to know that real-world volume ahead of testing live — this lets it be evaluated cheaply before committing to persistent storage and a retention policy. New `src/decode/stray_frame_log.py`, `GET /api/rf/stray-frames`.
- **Channel histogram's "no scan yet" message fixed to actually respect `hidden`.** Long-standing bug in `.rf-histogram-empty` (unrelated to the Stray Frames card above, just first noticed while live-testing it): the CSS unconditionally set `display: flex`, which overrides the browser's built-in `[hidden] { display: none }` regardless of specificity, so setting `hidden = true` from JS once a real histogram loaded never actually hid the message — it stayed visible and overflowed past its fixed-height wrapper into whatever card sat below it on the page. Added a `.rf-histogram-empty[hidden] { display: none; }` override.

#### Stats and node insights

- **Telemetry rows are now auto-pruned, closing the one table that could grow completely unbounded.** `packets` already had an automatic row-count cap and hourly cleanup (`max_packets_retained`, existing), but `telemetry` (battery/voltage/temperature/etc. history) had no retention at all — found while investigating a real "db grew a lot" report (23.7 MB in 3 days on a live 5-network box). New `max_telemetry_retained` config field (Configuration → Advanced → Storage, mirrors the existing packets field exactly) and `TelemetryRepository.cleanup_old()`, wired into the same already-running hourly cleanup loop — no new background task needed. `messages` (DM/channel chat history) and the node roster stay deliberately un-pruned; those are content you read, not a log.
- **Repeater Trends chart (and node drawer metrics) no longer silently truncate as history grows.** The Trends chart fetched with `hours=100000&limit=50000` as a deliberate "give me the entire history, however long it is" hack — but the underlying query was a plain `ORDER BY timestamp ASC LIMIT`, so once a repeater's telemetry history within the window exceeded the row cap, it silently returned the OLDEST rows and dropped the newest ones (the chart would quietly stop showing new data with no error anywhere). The busiest repeater on a real production box was already at ~10,000 rows, a fifth of the way to that cliff. `TelemetryRepository.get_history()` and `PacketRepository.get_signal_history()` now bucket into `limit` evenly-sized time windows (each point is that bucket's average) instead of returning raw rows — the returned point count stays bounded regardless of how long or dense the underlying history is, so a chart can never silently truncate again; `limit` is now a target point count, not a raw-row cap. Bucket width is derived from the actual span of matching data (new shared `src/storage/time_bucket.py`), not the requested `hours` window — sizing off the (deliberately oversized) requested window instead would have crushed a few weeks of real data into a handful of absurdly coarse buckets. Verified against a production database copy: the busiest repeater's ~10,000 raw rows resolve to 1000 well-distributed buckets spanning its full ~22-day history, with the newest bucket within 30 minutes of the true latest sample; sparse nodes, nodes with no history at all, and the normal node-drawer's short-window call are all unaffected.
- **Mesh topology graph.** A new **Topology** page (Networks sidebar group) draws the mesh as a live force-directed graph on a canvas — no mapping libraries, self-contained like the rest of the dashboard. Edges come from three sources already in the database: Meshtastic **traceroute** chains (every consecutive hop pair), **direct receptions** by this box (packets heard first-hand, with average RSSI/SNR), and the imported MeshCore **neighbour** star around your repeater (SNR per neighbour). Nodes are colored by protocol (this box gets a green ring, the neighbour-reporting repeater an amber one), labelled with their roster names, and sized by how connected they are; edge thickness tracks observation count and edges older than a week render dashed. Drag nodes to untangle, drag the background to pan, zoom with the scroll wheel or the +/− buttons, hover for details, toggle the three edge kinds with the header chips, and click the legend entries (this box / neighbour source / Meshtastic / MeshCore) to hide whole node classes and focus on one network at a time; the view auto-fits the whole graph once the layout settles, with a Fit button to re-center any time. Clicking a node spotlights its links and opens the regular node drawer (telemetry history, recent packets) — the same one the dashboard node cards use. A **Graph | Map** switch (persisted per browser, Graph by default) projects the same network onto the real map: nodes with known coordinates become markers on the dashboard's dark map tiles, edges become geographic lines — the repeater's neighbour star turns into an actual coverage picture — with the same colors, filters, tooltips, zoom/Fit buttons, and click-to-drawer working in both modes. Nodes without a position are honestly left off the map (a corner note counts them) rather than placed somewhere fake — and an **"all positions" layer toggle** (off by default) does the reverse: every positioned node *without* link evidence appears as a faint grey dot behind the linked skeleton, turning the map into a scouting tool for links you haven't proven yet. The graph builds at request time from stored packets (`GET /api/topology/graph`) and fills in on its own as traceroutes and neighbour imports accumulate. With repeater polling enabled, the graph also stays **live**: each poll now asks the repeater for its own neighbour list (`fetch_all_neighbours`, same logged-in session as status/telemetry, tolerant of firmware that lacks it), every polled repeater becomes its own star of SNR edges with skew-immune freshness timestamps, and the Repeaters page health card shows the fetched neighbour count. The Signal Intelligence section pairs the RSSI histogram with an SNR histogram (2 dB buckets over the last 500 packets), so noise-margin health is visible at a glance. An **Export PNG** button (Graph mode only) snapshots the current view — node/edge counts and a timestamp are stamped onto the image itself so it's self-contained outside the dashboard; Map mode is a separate Leaflet layer and isn't covered by this button yet.
- **Recent packets in the node drawer.** Opening a node now shows its last 15 packets (time, type, RSSI/SNR to one decimal) in a collapsible section, next to the existing metrics history; works for Meshtastic and MeshCore nodes alike.
- **Near-field packets no longer skew signal stats.** RSSI readings above −20 dBm (a node centimetres from the antenna during desk testing, or 0-dBm placeholders) are excluded from the Stats best/avg RSSI tiles and the RSSI histogram, so "Best RSSI" reflects actual reach.
- **Network totals no longer capped at 500 nodes.** The network summary (Stats page and `meshpoint report`) computed its totals over the 500 most recent nodes, silently under-reporting node counts, positions, and packet sums on larger installs; it now uses whole-table SQL aggregates.
- **Total Packets tile shows 24h / total.** The dashboard stat card now reads like the Nodes Discovered tile ("339 / 935"), pairing the last 24 hours with the all-time count.
- **"Farthest Direct Signal" no longer shows an imported repeater.** The fallback query behind this stat (used when no genuinely-captured direct reception exists yet) picked the max-distance `neighbour_advert` row with no regard for where the row came from — including historical MeshCore neighbour imports, which insert third-party observations with `hop_limit=0` (looks direct). A freshly-imported repeater 42 km away could outrank every packet this box has actually heard itself. The query now excludes both known import markers: `capture_source='meshcore_db_import'` (current `scripts/import_meshcore_db.py`) and the `nb:`/`meshcoredb:` `packet_id` prefixes (the actual marker on already-imported historical rows, from an earlier now-superseded import script) — genuine direct receptions never use either pattern.
- **Range card subtitles on the Stats page now say what they actually measure.** "Farthest Direct Signal" was labeled just "Received directly without relaying (0 hops)" — accurate but easy to misread as band- or protocol-specific; it's actually the single farthest zero-hop reception across every protocol/band this box listens to (Meshtastic or MeshCore only — LoRaWAN packets never get a position profile, so they can never appear here), tracked live for the current run. "Farthest MeshCore Contact" was the more misleading of the three: despite sitting next to two reception-based cards, it's not a reception measurement at all — it's the farthest node in your MeshCore roster with a known position, which can include imported or historical contacts you've never actually heard directly. Both subtitles now say so.
- **"Farthest Direct Signal" is now purely session-based, no DB fallback.** User noticed a node the Dashboard's Nodes panel correctly tagged DIRECT never showed up as "Farthest Direct Signal" on the Stats page — traced to the stat's DB-backed fallback (`_get_farthest_neighbour_direct()`, used when the live session accumulator has nothing yet) being hardcoded to `packet_type = 'neighbour_advert'`, MeshCore-only, so a Meshtastic direct contact could never satisfy it regardless of distance or recency. First fix broadened the fallback to match by hop count (`hop_start = 0` or `hop_start = hop_limit`, the same definition the Dashboard's own DIRECT filter uses) instead of packet type — but this surfaced a physically implausible 743 km "direct, no relay" MeshCore contact with a strong clean SNR, exposing a deeper problem: `hop_start`/`hop_limit` default to `0`/`0` on several packet paths that are *not* genuine direct receptions (confirmed live repeater-neighbour-poll rows default to the identical 0/0 and were only ever excluded from the old fallback by a coincidental `nb:`-prefixed packet_id convention, not by anything hop-related) — hop count alone isn't a trustworthy signal of "really heard directly" across every row in the table. Removed the DB fallback entirely rather than keep patching it; "Farthest Direct Signal" now only ever reflects `StatsReporter`'s live, real-time hop accounting for packets actually decoded this session — it can legitimately read "--" right after a restart until something genuinely direct is heard again, which is more honest than a DB query second-guessing historical hop metadata.

#### Configuration and server

- **Named, revocable API keys for Meshpoint's read-only status routes.** `require_auth` on `/metrics` previously only accepted the dashboard's own session cookie or a short-lived session Bearer JWT, which is awkward for an unattended scraper (Home Assistant, Prometheus) that can't hold a browser login. Configuration → Metrics now has an "API keys" panel: generate a labelled key (e.g. "Home Assistant"), copy the raw value shown once (only its SHA-256 hash is ever stored, matching how admin passwords are handled), and send it as `Authorization: Bearer <key>`. Each key is scoped to a small fixed allowlist — `/metrics`, plus (new) `GET /api/device/metrics` (host CPU/RAM/disk/temp/fan) and `GET /api/stats/summary` (best signal ever, farthest contact, node role/hardware-model distribution) — never general dashboard access, config mutation, or mesh control. Individually revocable, takes effect immediately with no restart. New `MetricsApiKey` config model (`metrics.api_keys`), `POST`/`DELETE /api/config/metrics/api-keys`, shared `src/api/auth/metrics_api_key.py` dependency used by all three routes.
- **Fresh installs no longer crash `GET /api/config`.** On a new box whose `local.yaml` has a bare `meshcore.private_channels:` (or `channel_keys:`) key, YAML parses the value as null, overwriting the config's empty-list default — every dashboard page then hit a 500 (`'NoneType' object is not iterable`) when loading configuration. Both fields are now null-guarded in the endpoint.
- **Installer ships the lgpio build dependencies.** `pip install lgpio` (fan/LED/button support) compiles a C extension that needs `swig` + `python3-dev` to build and `liblgpio-dev` to link — previously documented in TROUBLESHOOTING.md but missing from `scripts/install.sh`, so fresh installs and upgrades died at "Setting up Python virtual environment" with `error: command 'swig' failed`. The installer now apt-installs all three, both in the main package list and before the upgrade fast-path's early pip refresh — and also ships `ffmpeg`, which the RTL-SDR listener's audio pipeline needs.
- **Installer sets up RTL-SDR support end to end.** Previously entirely manual per box: `librtlsdr` wasn't installed at all, the dongle had no udev permissions, and the kernel's own DVB driver stack (`dvb_usb_rtl28xxu` plus the `rtl_2832`/`rtl_2830` demodulator modules it depends on) would claim the RTL2832U chip before rtl-sdr's userspace tools (`rtl_fm`/`rtl_test`) could open it. The installer now blacklists all three kernel modules (and unloads them immediately if already loaded this boot, bridge module first since it depends on the demodulator modules, so a reboot isn't required to test), then clones and builds `rtl-sdr` from source (osmocom upstream, `cmake -DINSTALL_UDEV_RULES=ON`) rather than `apt install rtl-sdr` — matching the existing SX1302 HAL build's build-from-source pattern, and leaving room to swap in a vendor fork later (e.g. RTL-SDR Blog's own fork for their V4/R828D dongle) without an apt package fighting it. Both steps are idempotent (skips the blacklist file if already present, skips the clone+build if `librtlsdr` is already installed) — safe to re-run on upgrade. The `meshpoint` service user's `plugdev` group membership (needed for device access) was already handled elsewhere in the installer.
- **Installer builds redsea, the RTL-SDR RDS decoder.** Adds a `scripts/install.sh` step (right after the rtl-sdr build) that apt-installs `meson`/`libsndfile1-dev`/`libliquid-dev` and then clones and builds `redsea` (windytan/redsea upstream) via `meson setup build && meson compile && meson install`, giving the Radio tab's FM listener access to station name, radio text, and PI code decoding on top of the librtlsdr built in the previous step. Idempotent — skips the clone+build if a `redsea` binary is already on `PATH`.
- **Installer sets up mDNS (Avahi) so the box is reachable as `meshpoint.local`.** Previously an IP address was the only way to reach a fresh box — awkward right after flashing, before a static IP/DHCP reservation exists, and for the Home Assistant integration's setup step, which asks for a host. `apt install avahi-daemon avahi-utils` + `systemctl enable --now avahi-daemon`, idempotent (skips the apt install if `avahi-daemon` is already present).
- **Unmapped Meshtastic channel hashes no longer silently blend into LongFast's message history — and no longer vanish from the Messages sidebar either.** `ChannelHashResolver.lookup()` used to fall back to channel index 0 for any `channel_hash` it couldn't map to a configured channel — meaning traffic on a channel this box doesn't have configured (a config mismatch, e.g. the same PSK reused under a different channel name on another node) looked identical to genuine LongFast messages, with nothing distinguishing them apart. Confirmed this masked a real mismatch for weeks in one case. `lookup()` now returns `None` for an unmapped hash instead of `0`, and the caller (`on_text_packet` in `server.py`) routes it to its own distinct conversation — `broadcast:meshtastic:unmapped:0xHH`. Live-testing the backend fix surfaced a second bug in the same feature: the Messages sidebar's "Channels" section rendered exclusively from the configured `/api/messages/channels` list, and "Direct Messages" explicitly excludes anything broadcast — so a correctly-routed unmapped conversation had nowhere to render at all, silently invisible despite being correctly stored and correctly kept out of LongFast. Added a third sidebar section, "Unmapped," in `messaging_contacts.js` specifically for broadcast conversations that exist in stored messages but aren't in the configured channel list. A warning still logs once per unique unmapped hash (existing throttle, unchanged) to avoid flooding logs on a channel with ongoing unmapped traffic. Live-testing also caught a third bug: replying from an Unmapped conversation used `convo.channel || 0` in `messaging.js`, and no `Conversation` object actually has a `channel` field, so every reply silently transmitted on channel 0 (LongFast) instead of failing — the exact silent-wrong-channel bug this feature was built to eliminate on receive, reappearing on send. Fixed by disabling the input/Send button entirely whenever a conversation is genuinely unmapped.
- **Meshpoint can now reply correctly to a channel whose PSK it has configured under a different local name, instead of just refusing to send.** An "unmapped" hash almost always means the remote node uses the same shared key under a channel name typed differently on their side (e.g. their "PD2EMC" is this box's "Home") — the packet decrypts fine, it just fails the exact-hash lookup. `meshtastic_decoder.py`'s existing key brute-force loop already tried every configured key and knew which one worked, but discarded that fact once decryption succeeded; it's now recorded on the `Packet` as `matched_channel_index`. When a hash is unmapped but a key still matched, `on_text_packet` routes it to a distinct "keyed" conversation (`broadcast:meshtastic:keyed:{index}:0x{hash}`) encoding both which local key/channel to reply with and the exact hash byte the sender expects — recomputing our own hash from our own channel name would produce a value their radio doesn't recognize, since Meshtastic's channel_hash is a lossy one-way digest of name XOR key, not reversible back to a name. `tx_service.send_text()` gained an `echo_hash` parameter that stamps the outgoing packet with this exact byte while still encrypting with the correct key; the messaging UI now shows these as a "Different Channel Name" sidebar section with replying enabled, instead of the disabled "Unmapped" state from the previous fix. **Live-tested and confirmed**: a reply sent from this conversation arrived correctly in the Tag's own channel thread, not LongFast. A live follow-up test then caught a fourth bug in the same conversation: after the reply sent successfully, the thread's title regressed from the sender's own name ("PD2EMC Meshtastic Tag") to the raw node_id string. Root cause: `MessageRepository.get_conversations()` grouped by `node_id` with a bare (non-aggregated) `node_name` column, so SQLite could pick that value from whichever row happened to be chronologically latest — a sent reply correctly saves `node_name=""` (there's no "sender" to name for something we sent), so the moment that reply became the newest message, the whole conversation's name reverted to blank even though a real name had been resolved moments earlier. This was never reachable before today, since these conversations couldn't be replied to at all until the previous fix landed. Fixed with a correlated subquery that picks the latest **non-blank** `node_name` per conversation independent of which row supplies the preview text/timestamp.
- **Fixed the 433 MHz Meshtastic USB stick misreading its own local channel-table index as a real over-the-air channel_hash, both receiving and sending.** meshtastic-python reports `packet["channel"]` as the connected stick's own channel-table slot (0-7) for anything it decoded locally with its own key — not the real on-air hash — but `serial_source.py` stuffed that value straight into the raw frame's hash-byte position, so the decoder read a small index as if it were a genuine hash and could misroute the conversation (or, worse, silently collide with an unrelated real channel whose hash happened to match a small number). Fixed by reading the stick's own channel table at connect time (index → name, falling back to the modem preset's display name for a blank primary channel, same convention firmware itself uses) and threading the resolved NAME through instead: `Packet` gained a `remote_channel_name` field, and `on_text_packet` now routes by that name first — landing in the matching Meshpoint channel's normal conversation if the names line up, or a clearly labeled `broadcast:meshtastic:named:{name}` bucket if they don't — rather than ever trusting the bare index as a hash. Sending had the mirror-image bug: replying via a serial stick passed Meshpoint's own channel index straight through as if it were that stick's index, though the two are separate physical nodes with independently-numbered channel tables. `tx_service.py` now translates by name (`resolve_channel_index()`) and refuses to send — rather than guessing — when the connected stick has no channel configured under that name at all.
- **Hardened `ChannelHashResolver.rebuild()` against a config/crypto ordering drift that already caused a real production mismatch (the inbound hash map and outbound TX computation disagreeing about which hash belonged to which channel index — 0xC9 vs 0x71 for the same config).** It previously paired the *i*-th channel name from the config's `channel_keys` dict with the *i*-th key from `crypto.get_all_keys()` — two independently-populated collections (`coordinator.py`'s startup loader vs `config_routes.py`'s live-update handlers) that only produce the right hash if both happen to iterate in the same order. Now looks up each channel's key by NAME directly in `crypto._keys`, immune to either collection's ordering. Also had to make sure this didn't introduce a different bug: `crypto._keys` is shared storage for both Meshtastic *and* MeshCore channel keys, so the lookup stays scoped to names actually present in the Meshtastic `channel_keys` dict passed in, rather than hashing in every key crypto happens to hold.
- **Installer builds multimon-ng, the RTL-SDR digital mode decoder.** Adds a `scripts/install.sh` step for POCSAG/AFSK/DTMF/etc decoding out of `rtl_fm`-piped audio. Built from source (EliasOenal/multimon-ng upstream) via CMake — the project dropped its old qt4-qmake build system entirely, so no Qt4 packages are pulled in (and `qt4-qmake` isn't even packaged in current Raspberry Pi OS repos anymore, so the classic qmake instructions floating around online would hard-fail a fresh install). Apt-installs `libpulse-dev`/`libx11-dev` for live audio input and the X11 scope display. Idempotent — skips the clone+build if a `multimon-ng` binary is already on `PATH`.
- **Installer installs rtl_433, a generic RTL-SDR OOK/FSK decoder.** Adds a `scripts/install.sh` step (right after multimon-ng) installing the Raspberry Pi OS `rtl-433` package with `apt install --no-install-recommends` — small (~500 KB) and current enough that a from-source build (like rtl-sdr/redsea/multimon-ng above) wasn't warranted; `--no-install-recommends` skips the optional soapysdr module packages, which nothing here uses. Covers a much broader device set than the P2000/Pagers/POCSAG multimon-ng pipelines — weather stations, TPMS, remote sensors, and hundreds of other 433/315/868 MHz OOK/FSK devices. No dashboard integration yet; this bullet is installer-only.
- **Installer installs the Meshtastic and MeshCore CLI tools.** Adds a `scripts/install.sh` step (right after rtl_433) installing `meshtastic-cli` (`pip3 install --upgrade "meshtastic[cli]" --break-system-packages`, needed since Debian's system Python is PEP 668-protected) and `meshcore-cli` (`pipx install meshcore-cli`, in its own isolated venv — `pipx` is now installed as a system package alongside the other build tools). Neither is used by Meshpoint itself (which talks to radios directly via meshtastic-python/meshcore-python), just handy for admin debugging straight from the Pi's shell.
- **Installer adds a fastfetch login banner.** Appends `fastfetch` to the `pi` user's `~/.bashrc`, so every interactive SSH/console login shows the system-info splash (OS, uptime, CPU temp/load, RAM, interfaces, etc) instead of needing to run it manually. Idempotent — skips if the line is already present.
- **Quieter boot log.** The MeshCore contact sync logged the companion's entire roster — 350 lines per boot on a well-connected stick. It now logs the peer count, the first 10 names, and "… and N more"; the full roster stays browsable on the MeshCore page.
- **Startup banner: one line per capture source.** The banner's single Source/Frequency pair (which only showed the concentrator's Meshtastic channel) is replaced by a per-source list with each radio's real plan: the concentrator's LoRaWAN span + Meshtastic service channel, each MeshCore companion's frequency/SF from its connect handshake, and each Meshtastic USB stick's resolved frequency and region. Sources still handshaking show "(radio info pending)". The logo box's right border also lines up with its corners again.
- **Web server port is now set in the config.** The dashboard bind address comes from `dashboard.host` / `dashboard.port` in the YAML config (override in `local.yaml`, applied on service restart) via the new `src/serve.py` launcher; previously the port was hardcoded in the systemd unit and the config value only affected the startup banner. If the config fails to load, or the configured address cannot be bound (port in use, privileged port, bad host), the server falls back to `0.0.0.0:8080` so the dashboard (and its update/rollback page) stays reachable.
- **Relay burst and RSSI filters editable in Configuration → Transmit.** Burst size and the min/max RSSI relay window (only packets heard inside the window are rebroadcast) can now be set from the dashboard; previously these existed in `local.yaml` and the relay API but had no UI.
- **MeshCore channel limit raised from 7 to 40 user channels.** The configuration card, YAML `meshcore.channel_keys`, and companion slot sync now accept up to 40 user channels (slots 1–40; slot 0 stays Public), up from 7.
- **Unused API endpoints removed.** `GET /api/packets/protocols`, `/api/packets/types`, `/api/nodes/map`, and `/api/telemetry/{id}` (+`/history`) served data already available through `/api/stats/summary`, `/api/nodes`, and `/api/nodes/{id}/metrics_history`; nothing in the dashboard or CLI used them.
- **Prometheus metrics gets a dashboard config page.** `metrics:` was the last config section with no UI at all — enabling the `/metrics` scrape endpoint meant hand-editing `local.yaml`. New **Configuration → Metrics** page toggles `enabled` and `require_auth`; unlike most config pages, both apply immediately (`metrics_routes.py` reads the config live on every request), no restart needed. New `PUT /api/config/metrics`, and `GET /api/config` now includes a `metrics` summary.
- **Configuration sidebar's Companions get their own sub-group, plus a new POCSAG companion config page.** The Configuration section's flat 12-item list is now split into labeled sub-groups (Companions: MeshCore/Serial/POCSAG; Network: MQTT/Repeater Poll; Hardware: GPS/Peripherals; System: Advanced/Metrics), with Transmit promoted up next to Radio since it's core radio behavior, not a companion. New **Configuration → POCSAG** page (mirrors the Serial/Meshtastic card, minus the identity/advert concept a POCSAG board has no use for) edits up to 4 `extra/pocsag_companion` USB devices — label, serial port (shared port-picker datalist across all three USB companion protocols), baud, and a free-text display name. `capture.pocsag_serial` persists via a new `PUT /api/config/capture/pocsag-serial-devices` (config-only at the time this bullet was first written; see the DAPNET section above for the capture source that now consumes it).
- **Configuration → MeshCore can now change a companion's radio frequency/bandwidth/SF/CR directly from the dashboard**, same "Radio settings" card layout as Configuration → Serial's own Region control (preset select + Set button). Picks from the same full 20-entry MeshCore community preset list `meshpoint meshcore-radio` offers (see the CLI section below) via a new `PUT /api/config/meshcore/companion-radio`. Unlike the standalone CLI — which has to stop the whole meshpoint service and cold-connect a second process within a fixed handshake window, something that can fail outright on ESP32-S3 boards needing longer to come back up — this goes through the companion's own already-open connection and hands recovery to `MeshcoreUsbCaptureSource`'s existing battle-tested reconnect loop (exponential backoff + DTR reset pulse) once the post-change reboot drops it. Not persisted to `local.yaml`, same reasoning as Serial's Region: the setting lives durably in the companion's own flash.
- **A MeshCore companion whose command channel silently dies no longer stays stuck "connected" forever.** Found live testing the radio-settings card above: a companion whose command/request channel stopped responding kept reporting `connected: true` — passive RX still flowed, so the health-check loop's "skip the probe if there's been recent activity" optimization never triggered its own recovery — while every dashboard action against it (rename, radio change, health probes) timed out indefinitely with nothing to fix it short of a manual USB unplug. `SendResult` gained a `timed_out` field, distinct from a plain failure: a firmware ERROR response (e.g. "name in use") means the connection is healthy and just rejected the request, but a timeout means no answer came back at all within the deadline — real evidence the connection itself is wedged. Every per-companion command path (rename, radio params, advert, direct message, channel message) now treats a timeout exactly like the radio card's own post-reboot handling: mark disconnected and kick off the same backoff+DTR-reset reconnect loop immediately, instead of waiting on a health check that ongoing RX can mask indefinitely.
- **MeshCore USB reconnect attempts can no longer run two at once.** A side effect of the previous fix: a command timeout's immediate reconnect could fire while the health-check loop's own independent reconnect was already in flight, both racing to `_disconnect()`/`_connect()` the same serial port and each potentially pulsing the DTR reset line. New `_reconnect_in_progress` guard makes `_reconnect()` a no-op if one is already running, regardless of which of the (now three) triggers called it. Confirmed live during the same investigation that DTR is the one thing MeshCore's capture source touches that neither Meshtastic's serial source nor the DAPNET companion's protocol ever does — the same board/port/cable that misbehaved under MeshCore worked fine under both other firmwares — so cutting down on redundant DTR pulses is a real fix, not just tidiness.

#### CLI

- **`meshpoint report` works again.** The CLI report had been broken since API auth landed — every request got 401 and the command misreported "service is not running". It now prompts for dashboard admin credentials and uses a session cookie; `meshpoint status` distinguishes "running, login required" from "unreachable". Running it as root (`sudo meshpoint report`) skips the prompt entirely: with read access to the on-disk signing key the CLI mints its own short-lived admin token — same trust model as `meshpoint reset-password`, no server-side bypass.
- **`meshpoint report` covers all networks.** New PROTOCOLS section (one line per network: packets, nodes/devices, frequency/SF, TX/sniff status) and CAPTURE SOURCES section (SX1302 channel usage, MeshCore companions with serial port and name, last band sweep); the old RADIO CONFIG section slimmed to Meshtastic TX facts, and a MESHCORE section mirrors it (companion state and name, radio settings, TX power, channel list).
- **`meshpoint report`'s CAPTURE SOURCES section now lists Meshtastic USB serial sticks.** Previously only enumerated the concentrator and MeshCore companions — a connected serial Meshtastic radio (e.g. a Heltec V3) produced no line at all, even though `GET /api/config` already shipped its live connection state. Now reads that same `serial` list and prints one line per stick: frequency/SF, connected/disconnected, and the stick's own long name.
- **`meshpoint report` no longer merges two physically separate Meshtastic networks into one stat line.** A concentrator's own Meshtastic channel and a USB serial stick are usually on completely different frequencies (e.g. 868 MHz vs 433 MHz) — different meshes that can never talk to each other — but the PROTOCOLS section's packet/node counts were adding them together under one "Meshtastic" line. `packets.capture_source` was already tracked per-packet, so the fix is query-only: `PacketRepository.get_protocol_distribution_by_source()`/`get_distinct_node_count_by_source()` (new), wired through `/api/analytics/traffic`'s `meshtastic_by_source` and `/api/nodes/summary`'s `meshtastic_nodes_by_source`. The report now prints one "Meshtastic" line per radio once a second source shows up in the packet history, and a new MESHTASTIC SERIAL section (mirroring MESHCORE) lists each stick's radio settings, primary channel, and node ID. Single-radio boxes are unaffected — one source means one merged line, same as before.
- **`meshpoint meshcore-radio` now offers the full MeshCore community preset list** (20 regions — Australia's 5 sub-presets, Brazil, Czech Republic, both EU/UK variants, both EU 433MHz variants, Netherlands, both New Zealand variants, both Portugal variants, Switzerland, USA/Canada, both Vietnam variants) instead of just US/EU/ANZ, transcribed directly from the official MeshCore client's own "Select Radio Settings" picker so the numbers match what a real MeshCore user would pick. `US`/`EU`/`ANZ` still work as short aliases for their closest equivalents (USA/Canada, EU/UK Narrow, Australia Narrow — the exact values the old 3-entry table used, unchanged) so nothing that referenced them by name breaks. Notably fills a real gap: there was previously no 433 MHz preset at all, despite 433 MHz companions already being supported (Configuration → Serial/POCSAG).

#### Dashboard and UI

- **Names in the Meshtastic packets feed.** The Meshtastic page's Recent Packets showed bare hex node IDs even when the node census knew the name. Source and destination now resolve to the node's name with the ID dimmed alongside, and the page order now matches the MeshCore page: Recent Packets on top, the node census below. The MeshCore page's destination column gained the same name lookup (its source column already had it), and its type badges now wear the same colors as the Meshtastic page (nodeinfo amber, text cyan, neighbour_advert green) instead of uniform gray. The LoRaWAN page follows the same order too: all three protocol pages now read Recent Packets first, node/device census below.
- **Fixed: the "Add to Home Screen" app icon looked noticeably smaller than every other icon next to it** (user's own comparison screenshot, next to WhatsApp). `frontend/assets/meshpoint-logo.png` (the `apple-touch-icon` source) turned out to be an exported "icon preview mockup" rather than raw full-bleed artwork -- it already had its own rounded-square shape baked in, sitting in the middle of a mostly-transparent 256×256 canvas: the visible content only covered ~54% of the image (~58px of transparent padding on every side). iOS then treats the *whole* file as the icon and applies its own rounding/mask on top of that already-small, already-rounded interior graphic, shrinking it further. Fixed by cropping to the actual content's bounding box and re-scaling to fill the canvas edge to edge -- the mark now fills 100% of the image, matching how full-bleed icons are supposed to be supplied (the OS does its own corner-rounding; apps aren't meant to pre-round or pad). One real quality tradeoff worth knowing: the only source available was this same small raster (~140px of real content), so filling the frame is an upscale, not new detail -- the fine line/text edges are a little softer than a from-scratch full-resolution export would give, most visible at the largest (512px) size. Also added the manifest.json Android/Chrome's own "Add to Home Screen" flow needs and never had -- previously only `apple-touch-icon` was wired up (iOS-only); `<link rel="manifest">` + `<meta name="theme-color">` (matching the dashboard's own `--bg-primary: #0a0e17`) now point at a new `frontend/manifest.json` with properly-sized `icon-192.png`/`icon-512.png` (same crop-and-fill treatment, generated at their own native resolutions rather than just scaling the 256px file down/up). Verified: `manifest.json` parses as valid JSON, all three icon files' alpha bounding box now spans the full canvas (no leftover transparent margin), `test_html_assets` (index.html asset-URL rewriting) still passes unchanged. **Same-day follow-on, a real regression caught live**: `meshpoint-logo.png` isn't only the `apple-touch-icon` source -- the sidebar also renders it as the dashboard's own visible logo (`.sidebar__logo` in `frontend/sidebar/sidebar.css`), and that CSS had special compensation logic tuned to the *old* padded image's exact geometry: it rendered the `<img>` at 84×84 (1.5x the 56×56 frame) and `clip-path: inset(14px round 14px)`'d it back down, deliberately "zooming into" the ~25-30% built-in padding so the mark would fill the frame despite the source image not being full-bleed (the rule's own comment even said as much: "adjust the inset down if a tighter PNG asset is shipped later"). Once the source became genuinely full-bleed, that same oversized-render-plus-crop started cutting into the *actual* logo instead of empty padding -- the "Meshpoint" wordmark got clipped off the bottom in the sidebar. Fixed by removing the compensation entirely: `.sidebar__logo` now renders at the frame's own 56×56 with no `clip-path`, which is all a full-bleed image needs.
- **Fixed: reloading on any page other than Dashboard briefly flashed the Dashboard section before "jumping" to the actual page.** User's report, reproduced on every hard reload of e.g. `#/settings/updates`. Root cause: `frontend/index.html`'s Dashboard `<section>` is the only one shipped without `style="display:none"` in the raw HTML (so the first paint is fast) -- every other section starts hidden and only gets shown by `sidebar/sidebar_controller.js`'s `_renderActive(route)`, which doesn't run until the very last of the page's ~122 `<script>` tags (`js/app.js`) has loaded and constructed the router. So every reload painted Dashboard first, then corrected to the real route once all of that finished loading -- the flash. Fixed with a small inline `<script>` right after the section markup, before any of those 122 scripts start loading: it reads `location.hash` once and immediately sets `display` on the matching `[data-section]` element, the same match `_renderActive()` does later -- so the correct section is what actually paints first, no loading screen needed. Doesn't touch routing/auth at all; the real router still runs identically a moment later (an admin-only route deep-linked by a viewer briefly shows that section's inert, dataless skeleton instead of Dashboard's before being redirected to forbidden, same as today -- every section's skeleton already sits inert in the DOM regardless of role). Verified: a standalone run of the inline script's matching logic against three cases (a real route, an empty hash, an unknown hash) all resolve exactly as intended; `test_html_assets` (index.html asset-URL rewriting, unaffected since this script has no `src`) still passes.
- **Tab switch on all protocol pages.** Instead of two stacked tables, each protocol page now has one panel with a tab switch — Recent Packets | Contacts (MeshCore), | Nodes (Meshtastic), | Devices (LoRaWAN) — each view getting the full height. Both views keep refreshing in the background so switching is instant, and the chosen tab persists per page across visits. The census tables lead with time now too: Last heard first on MeshCore contacts and Meshtastic nodes, Last seen then First seen first on LoRaWAN devices.
- **Messages tab shows overheard DMs by default.** "Monitor mode" (the eye icon) previously defaulted off and never persisted, so on a box that's typically deployed as a repeater/observer — never itself a DM party — nearly all DM traffic it sees is classified "overheard" and the tab looked empty on every single visit until the icon was clicked. It now defaults to on; the icon still lets you hide overheard DMs again if you want a quieter view.
- **Favorite channels in the Messages tab.** Channels were always listed in the server's config order (`channel_keys` insertion order) with no way to change that per browser. Each channel row now has a star toggle — favorited channels pin to the top (in the order you starred them), everything else keeps the existing config order below. Per-browser via `localStorage`, mirroring the Node Cards favorites feature's exact shape (same cap, same change-event pattern) rather than inventing a new one. No drag-and-drop reordering — a pin/favorite was simpler to build well and covers the actual ask ("I want my channel(s) first"), not a full manual ranking of every channel. A new **Fav** filter next to All/MT/MC shows only favorited channels (no DMs).
- **MeshCore channel order is now editable from Configuration → MeshCore.** Up/down arrows next to each channel row reorder them (Public always stays first); Save Channels submits the new order and it's written to `local.yaml` exactly as arranged — no separate "order" field needed, `channel_keys` is a dict and Python/YAML already preserve insertion order end to end. This is the shared, admin-set order every browser sees by default; the per-browser channel favorites above sit on top of it as a personal override.
- **Packet detail modal everywhere.** Clicking a row in any packet feed — the Dashboard's live feed or the LoRaWAN, Meshtastic, and MeshCore pages — opens a full packet-detail breakdown (RF, mesh routing, decoded payload, capture metadata) without leaving the page. The protocol packet APIs return the full stored fields (hop start/limit, bandwidth, decoded payload, capture source) to feed it. The payload section is protocol-aware: MeshCore packets (decoded, not decrypted with a Meshtastic channel key) no longer show a misleading "Decrypt: No matching key" row and always display their decoded content. The Dashboard feed's modal now resolves From/To to node names (like the protocol pages already did) instead of showing bare short IDs, and the broadcast address shows as "broadcast" on every page. The Meshtastic and MeshCore packet APIs now also return the stored channel hash, relay byte, and want-ack, so a packet opened from a protocol page shows the same routing detail (Channel hash, Relay byte, channel label) as the live Dashboard feed instead of dropping those rows. MeshCore advertisements also surface a readable "Node type" row (Client / Repeater / Room server / Sensor) instead of leaving it as a bare integer in the payload JSON. Below the one-line Content summary the modal now adds an expandable "Details" view of the full decoded payload, so every field the summary drops (position sats/ground speed/precision, telemetry humidity/pressure/channel-utilisation/uptime, nodeinfo role/public key, …) is one click away on both the Dashboard and the protocol pages. Rows with no meaningful value are now hidden instead of printing an empty "n/a" or "(unknown)" — the Hops row on direct packets, and Modem/RSSI/SNR/Channel on bare LoRaWAN joins. The Dashboard feed's modal also stopped mangling non-hex identifiers: a LoRaWAN DevEUI ("A4:11:63:C3:00:01:2D:DE") or a literal like "network-server" now shows in full (matching the LoRaWAN page) instead of being truncated to a meaningless "!D:DE" / "!rver" short ID.
- **Consistent RSSI colors.** The Dashboard packet feed colored signal strength on a stricter scale (green only above −90 dBm) than the Meshtastic/MeshCore/LoRaWAN pages (green above −100 dBm), so the same packet showed amber on one page and green on another. The feed now uses the panels' bands — −100 dBm is still a comfortable LoRa signal. The node cards and node drawer quality tiers (Excellent/Good/Fair/Poor) are aligned to the same breakpoints too: Good now reaches down to −100 dBm and Fair to −115 (was −95/−110), so a −100 dBm node no longer wears an amber "Fair" chip next to a green feed row.
- **Topbar chips unified.** All three protocol chips render their name slot in the same plain style (the concentrator chip's node name and the USB chip's node ID were spaced-out glowing call-sign lettering; MeshCore's was plain), the chips dropped their region segment (EU_868/EU_433 — the frequency already tells the band), and the MeshCore chip's last separator became the same `|` bar the Meshtastic chips use. When the dashboard connection drops, all three now say "Reconnecting…" with blanked values in the same plain style (the concentrator chip used to keep showing stale values with only an amber lamp), restoring the real values when the connection returns.
- **Sidebar regrouped.** Dashboard on top, then **Networks** (LoRaWAN, Meshtastic, MeshCore, Messages, Stats), **Radio** (Hardware, RF Environment, RTL-SDR), and **Ops** (Terminal, Configuration, Settings). The former "Radio" page is now called **Hardware**, the listener appears as **RTL-SDR**, and the RF Environment tab lives in the Radio group instead of a link below the sidebar telemetry rail.
- **Inline modals instead of browser popups.** Confirmation dialogs in the update panel, channel and MeshCore configuration cards, sign-out-all, viewer-role form, and dangerous actions now use the dashboard's own modal styling instead of native `confirm()` popups.
- **Dates on packet feeds.** LoRaWAN, Meshtastic, and MeshCore panels show a date for packets from previous days ("Jul 5, 16:19"); today's packets keep the compact time-only form.
- **Home button on the node map.** A small house-icon button next to the expand (⤢) button in the Node Map panel header recenters the map on the Meshpoint's own configured location (`device.latitude`/`longitude`, zoom 14) on demand — a quick way back after panning around, without disturbing the existing "remember zoom/view across reload" behavior from v0.7.5. A stroke-style SVG (matching every other icon in the dashboard), not a color emoji — this UI doesn't use those anywhere else. Both header buttons now share a `.panel__header-actions` wrapper so they sit grouped at the right edge; without it, the header's `justify-content: space-between` treated a lone middle button as its own flex item and centered it awkwardly between the title and the expand button.
- **Theme toggle in the topbar.** Cycles the three dark themes (default, high-contrast, sunlight) with per-theme icon, in sync with the command palette.
- **Incoming-message notifications.** A new toast pops up in the dashboard corner when a message arrives — sender name and a snippet, click to jump straight to that conversation — with an optional soft notification sound (WebAudio-synthesised, no assets). Fires only for messages actually received (never your own sent messages or overheard monitor-mode traffic) and stays quiet while you're already looking at the Messages page; rapid bursts collapse into one toast with a "+N more" line instead of stacking. Popup and sound are independent switches under Settings → System → Message notifications (popup on, sound off by default), also in the command palette; both are per-browser preferences, so a desktop can ping while a phone stays silent. The sound has its own switch on purpose — enabling it doesn't opt you into the connect/disconnect UI sounds.
- **24-hour clock everywhere.** Packet feeds, panels, node drawer, charts, messaging, and update pages all render `hour12: false`. The P2000/Pagers/POCSAG/RTL433 message logs (built after this sweep) were missed and still showed 12-hour AM/PM — fixed, and the AM/PM suffix wrapping onto its own line (worse on RTL433, whose device model names like "Generic-Remote" are longer than the fixed FLEX/POCSAG protocol labels) is gone now that the extra token is dropped; the time and model columns were also widened so long values don't wrap either.
- **24-hour clock, three more stragglers.** A follow-up grep found the packet detail modal's timestamp (`packet_detail_modal.js`, all three fallback branches) and the MQTT configuration card's "connected since"/"last publish" times (`mqtt_card.js`) still had no `hour12` option at all, so they silently inherited the browser's OS locale (12-hour on a US-locale browser) instead of the 24-hour format the rest of the dashboard settled on. Also fixed the repeater list's "last seen" date, which was hardcoded to `en-US` (forcing MM/DD/YYYY) regardless of the viewer's own locale — it now lets the browser's locale decide date component order like every other date call in the codebase.
- **Metric defaults.** Display units default to Celsius and kilometers for new browsers; explicit imperial choices are kept.

#### Import and maintenance scripts

- **Contacts + neighbours import.** Root `import_contacts.py` imports MeshCore contacts and neighbours with synthetic neighbour-advert rows (SNR surfaced in panels), skew-immune `last_heard` anchored to the local clock, and authoritative timestamp upserts floored at real captures.
- **Repair and backfill tools.** `scripts/repair_neighbour_timestamps.py` fixes past/future neighbour timestamps; `scripts/backfill_meshcore_signal.py` stamps frequency/SF on older MeshCore rows.
- **`scripts/edit_contact.py`.** Interactive CLI to correct a node's stored details (long/short name, latitude/longitude/altitude) — e.g. a stale or wrong GPS fix on a node whose real location you know. Looks the node up and shows its current data, asks for confirmation before editing, then prompts field-by-field with the current DB value as the default (press Enter to keep it), and confirms the full change set before writing.
- **`scripts/dab_channel_scan.py`.** Standalone diagnostic that drives `welle-cli` directly across all 38 Band III DAB channels (`5A`-`13F`), polling each one's `/mux.json` for an ensemble label + decoded stations, so the dashboard's DAB+ channel presets can be picked from what this antenna actually receives instead of another location's scanner listing (the previous `6C` preset, sourced from a different city's scanner data, decoded nothing here). Stops early per channel once an ensemble and at least one station have decoded, rather than always waiting the full timeout. Prints a running per-channel log plus a final summary of every channel with content, its ensemble name, SNR, and station list. **Live full-scan result** (38 channels, ~13 min): only `7D` (MTVNL), `8B` (NH/Flevo), `11C` (commercial nationals), and `12C` (NPO) actually decoded anything at this antenna.
