Fixed a real bug the first full run surfaced: the station filter only checked for a truthy `url_mp3`, not also a non-empty label, so a few services with blank labels slipped into the printed list (visible as empty bullet lines in `7D`'s result) -- now requires both, matching `DabListener`'s own filter. `9C` read "nothing" on that same full run but decoded 15 stations fine (SNR 7 dB) when retested alone -- a false negative from back-to-back channel switching, not a real reception gap. Default `--timeout` bumped 20s -> 30s and the inter-channel settle gap 0.5s -> 1.5s to reduce this, and the docstring now calls out that a "nothing" result on a full scan is worth an isolated retest before writing a channel off. Current DAB+ presets (`7D`/`8B`/`9C`/`11C`/`12C`) already match every channel confirmed live at this antenna -- no preset changes needed, though their labels were refreshed to name real stations from the actual scan output (e.g. `9C` -> "Throwback/hits (Sublime, KINK, Qmusic Foute Uur...)") instead of the earlier, less precise cross-city guesses. **FOLLOW-UP:** the script now also writes its results to a JSON file (new `--output`/`-o` flag, default `dab_channel_scan.json`) covering every scanned channel (ensemble label, SNR, station list), not just console output -- so a scan's findings can be read back programmatically instead of hand-copied into the dashboard's preset array. **Second follow-up:** a real full-scan run showed `11C`'s ensemble label decoding as the literal generic string `"DAB+"` rather than a descriptive name -- new `ENSEMBLE_LABEL_OVERRIDES` dict in the script rewrites known generic labels to something useful (`"DAB+"` -> `"Commercial"`, matching the dashboard's existing preset name for that channel) in both console output and the JSON file. **Third follow-up:** the same run also showed `8B` decoding as `"8B N-H / Flevo"` -- some ensembles bake their own channel code into the label, redundant since the channel is already known. New `strip_channel_code()` helper strips a channel's own code (as a whole-word, case-insensitive match, so it works for whichever channel is actually being scanned, not just `8B`) plus any leftover separator punctuation/whitespace from either end. Runs before the `DAB+`->`Commercial` override so the two chain correctly. **Fourth follow-up:** a targeted retest showed `9C`'s ensemble broadcasts no real name at all -- the label decodes as literally just `"9C"`, so stripping the channel code used to leave nothing and fall back to the redundant bare code. New `NO_LABEL_PLACEHOLDER` makes this case explicit instead: `strip_channel_code()` now returns `"9C (no name broadcast -- set label in config)"` when stripping would leave nothing, flagging that a real label still needs to be set (a future dashboard admin-editable preset-label feature, not built yet) rather than silently showing the channel code as if it were a real name. **Fifth follow-up:** `--output`'s default changed from a bare `dab_channel_scan.json` in whatever directory the script happened to be run from, to `/opt/meshpoint/config/dab_channel_scan.json` -- a fixed, predictable location the dashboard can read from later (the actual GUI-consumption piece, further above, still isn't built). Missing parent directories are now created automatically (`os.makedirs(..., exist_ok=True)`) so this doesn't fail on a fresh install where `config/` might not exist yet, or when overriding `--output` to a scratch path during testing. **Sixth follow-up:** user noticed rescanning a single channel (or a small subset) to chase this same false-negative flakiness was overwriting the whole file, losing every previously-found channel. Results now merge into `--output` by default: existing channels keyed by code, this run's results upsert into that map (updating an already-present channel in place, adding a new one, leaving every untouched channel exactly as it was), sorted back into raster order (`channel_sort_key()`, by position in the 5A-13F list rather than plain string order, where e.g. `"10A"` would otherwise sort before `"5A"`) before writing. New `--new` flag discards the existing file instead of merging, for a genuine fresh start. Each channel entry also gained its own `scanned_at` timestamp (the merged file's previous top-level `scanned_at` was renamed `last_run_at`, since with merging it only ever describes the most recent run, not every entry in the file). Lets a full station list be built up gradually across many small/targeted runs instead of needing one ~19-minute full scan. Verified end to end with a real (not bypassed) multi-run simulation: an initial 2-channel scan, a merge-in of a 3rd channel, an in-place update of an already-present channel with new SNR/stations, and a `--new` run confirmed to wipe and start over. **Seventh follow-up, same day:** the channel-level upsert above still had a gap -- a rescan that decoded fewer stations than a previous run (e.g. `9C` dropping from 15 stations to 8 because the scan exits early once it finds *any* station rather than waiting for all of them) or that failed entirely (transient dongle hiccup) would silently overwrite the better existing data, working against the whole point of merging. New `merge_channel_result()` makes the per-channel merge additive instead of a flat overwrite: station lists union (existing plus any newly-seen names, order-preserving, deduped) rather than replace, and a "nothing" rescan (empty ensemble and stations) leaves the existing entry completely untouched rather than erasing known-good data with a blank one. Verified against the exact reported scenario (an existing 15-station `9C` entry rescanned down to an 8-station subset stays at all 15) plus edge cases: a genuinely new station appends to the union, a "nothing" rescan is a full no-op, and a channel whose only prior entry was itself an empty placeholder correctly picks up real content once found. Also re-ran the full multi-run end-to-end simulation with two successive partial rescans of the same channel finding different single stations each time, confirming both accumulate into the merged file rather than the second replacing the first.
#### SenseCap M1 hardware

- **SenseCap M1 onboard LED/button/fan GPIO probe.** No public schematic exists for this board's expansion peripherals; new `scripts/test_gpio_hardware.py` (`gpiozero`, not a runtime dependency) identifies and exercises them. `led`/`button`/`fan` test one pin directly; `button-scan`/`fan-scan` sweep a batch of candidate pins at once (skipping the concentrator's SPI0 bus, the I2C crypto/temp chips, the HAT ID pins, and the concentrator reset lines) rather than guessing pin-by-pin. Confirmed live on real hardware: LED = GPIO 22, button = GPIO 27, fan = GPIO 13.
- **Configuration → Peripherals page.** Edits the SenseCap M1's onboard fan/LED/button settings (`fan:`/`led:`/`button:` in `local.yaml`) from the dashboard instead of hand-editing YAML — one form per peripheral (enable toggle, GPIO pin, and each peripheral's own tuning fields: fan's temp curve/duty/hysteresis, LED's activity-blink flicker, button's hold time and advert cooldown). New `PUT /api/config/hardware/{fan,led,button}`, always flags `restart_required` since all three only start once at app boot. Named "Peripherals" rather than "Hardware" — that name was already taken by the top-level Radio/concentrator page.
- **Temperature-driven PWM fan control.** New opt-in `fan:` config section drives the SenseCap M1's onboard fan from CPU temperature (`/sys/class/thermal/thermal_zone0/temp`) instead of running it flat-out or not at all. GPIO 13 is a hardware-PWM-capable pin on the Pi 4 (BCM2711 PWM1), so speed ramps linearly between `min_temp_c`/`max_temp_c` rather than a blunt on/off relay; a `hysteresis_c` gap and a `min_duty` floor (most small fans stall below some duty rather than spinning slower) avoid chatter and stalling right at the threshold. New `src/hardware/fan_control.py` (`FanCurve` for the pure duty-cycle math, `FanController` for the polling loop), runs as a background task for the app's lifetime same as the noise-floor emitter. Disabled by default — this hardware doesn't exist on RAK V2/Chameleon/DIY builds. `fan: {enabled: true}` alone is sufficient; every other key has a matching default, also documented (with inline comments) in `config/default.yaml` so the full set of knobs is discoverable without reading source. Caught before release: `_apply_yaml`'s `section_map` (the dict `local.yaml`/`default.yaml` sections get merged through) is manually maintained rather than derived from `AppConfig`'s fields, and `fan` was missing from it — the whole section was being silently ignored, so `enabled: true` would have done nothing at all. Fixed, with a regression test asserting `fan:` in `local.yaml` actually reaches `cfg.fan`. New `gpiozero`/`lgpio` runtime dependencies (`requirements.txt`) — `lgpio` specifically because gpiozero's pure-Python fallback pin factory (used when no real GPIO backend is installed) only allows PWM on pins in its hardcoded per-Pi-model table, and rejects a custom carrier board's repurposed GPIO with `PinPWMUnsupported` even though it's a genuine PWM-capable SoC pin; `lgpio` doesn't have that restriction. `FanController` now detects that specific exception and logs the `pip install lgpio` fix directly instead of a raw traceback. Live-verified the full install chain on a real Bookworm/trixie SenseCap M1: `pip install lgpio` builds a C extension with no piwheels wheel available, needing `python3-dev` + `swig` (build tools) and `liblgpio-dev` (the native `liblgpio.so` the extension links against — `cannot find -llgpio` without it) installed via `apt` first; documented as one block in `TROUBLESHOOTING.md`. One more gap surfaced after that: `lgpio` creates its notification pipe directly in `WorkingDirectory` (`/opt/meshpoint`), but `meshpoint.service`'s `ExecStartPre` only ever chowned `config/` and `data/` to the `meshpoint` service user, never the top-level directory — so it still fell back to the PWM-incapable pin factory with `xCreatePipe: ... Operation not permitted`. Fixed in `meshpoint.service` (`ExecStartPre` now hands the whole install tree to the service user recursively — see the self-update bullet below for why recursive), self-healing on every start regardless of how the checkout was deployed. Live-verified working end to end: `Fan control started on GPIO13` with no exception. The duty-change log line stays at `debug` (it was temporarily `info` to verify the ramp live, but with normal temperature jitter it fires on most 10-second polls — thousands of journal lines a day); the dashboard's Fan card is the live view. New stats-bar **Fan** card (after Load Avg) shows the current duty percentage and what it changed from (`"was 35%"`), hidden entirely when fan control isn't enabled; backed by new `fan_duty_percent`/`fan_previous_duty_percent` fields on `GET /api/device/metrics`, sourced from `FanController.current_duty`/`previous_duty` (only updated on an actual change, not every poll, so "previous" reflects the last real transition). Live logs then showed `(was X)` values disagreeing with the previously printed duty (and "changes" logged when nothing visibly changed): the controller compared the freshly computed full-precision duty against the pin's read-back value, which `lgpio` quantizes differently. It now rounds the duty to the 1% steps the log and dashboard display and compares against its own last-set value, so consecutive log lines agree and identical polls stay silent.
- **User button.** New opt-in `button:` config section gives the SenseCap M1's case button (GPIO 27, confirmed via the GPIO probe script) two gestures. Short press: advert on every TX-capable radio — concentrator Meshtastic NodeInfo, MeshCore companion advert, and each Meshtastic USB stick broadcasting its own NodeInfo — serialized 2 s apart because the two 868 MHz signals overlap outright (869.525/BW250 contains 869.618/BW62.5) and same-box TX deafens the neighbouring receiver; a 30 s cooldown stops advert spam, and LoRaWAN stays out by design (pure listener). Hold 3 s: restart the meshpoint service — the recovery that works when the dashboard doesn't; fired detached so it survives its own process dying, sudoers rule already shipped. The status LED narrates every gesture (ack double-blink, cooldown-denied long blink, fast-blink hold warning), and the controller boots disarmed so a button held straight through the restart it triggered can never re-trigger. Poll-based state machine, same testable pattern as the fan and LED. New `src/hardware/button_control.py`; documented in `config/default.yaml` and `docs/CONFIGURATION.md`.
- **Status LED.** New opt-in `led:` config section drives the SenseCap M1's onboard case LED (GPIO 22, confirmed via the GPIO probe script) as a glanceable status light with four states: steady on = service running and every configured capture source healthy; a brief off-flicker per captured packet (a router-style traffic dip — `activity_blink: false` for a calm steady light); 1 Hz blink = one or more capture sources down; dark = service not running (free — the kernel releases the GPIO line when the process dies). Plain on/off GPIO, deliberately no PWM, so it works even without `lgpio`. Health reads the same per-source running flags the capture pipeline maintains, and packet activity polls the existing stats counter at 10 Hz — the capture hot path is untouched. New `src/hardware/led_status.py`, documented in `config/default.yaml` and `docs/CONFIGURATION.md`.

#### MeshCore repeaters

- **Sensors card no longer blanks after a restart.** A poll can succeed on status but return empty telemetry (the companion still settling right after a service restart); that OK-but-empty result used to overwrite the previously stored sensor readings, leaving "No sensor telemetry" until the next full poll cycle. The poller now keeps the last real sensor data whenever a newer poll has none, failed or not.
- **MeshCore repeater monitoring.** New opt-in `repeater_poll:` config section periodically queries MeshCore repeaters you operate for their status and telemetry — the same `req_status`/`req_telemetry` calls the phone app and `meshcore-cli` make, through the companion Meshpoint already holds. MeshCore nodes advertise identity only (unlike Meshtastic's broadcast telemetry), so this fills the otherwise-empty repeater stats: battery, uptime, airtime, packet counters (flood/direct), noise floor, and LPP sensors (temp/humidity/pressure). Results show on a new **Repeaters** page (Radio sidebar group, visible only when polling is configured): per repeater, a **Health** card (battery, uptime, airtime, packet counters, noise floor, SNR, errors), a **Sensors** card listing every LPP reading it reports (all channels — temperature/humidity/pressure/altitude/solar), a **History** card (min/avg/max over stored telemetry), and a full-width **Trends** chart plotting the voltage, temperature, humidity and pressure history (rendered by the shared node-drawer chart, legend-toggleable; humidity and pressure were added to that chart so both the repeater trends and the Meshtastic node drawer gain them when a node reports them). The charted fields flow into the telemetry table for the node drawer and CSV export. Active two-way RF, so it's off by default, polls sequentially on a slow cadence, and only targets repeaters you have the login password for; passwords live in `local.yaml` and are never exposed by the API. A poll that fails transiently (the companion's command channel momentarily busy) is retried up to 3 times with a short gap before giving up. Zero-value sensor channels (an unused solar input at 0 V / 0 A / 0 W) are hidden from the Sensors card, and the cards read as a stats page — a full-width Health / Sensors / History row with a channel/value count chip and a Trends chart below. New `src/hardware/`-style `src/transmit/repeater_poller.py` + `GET /api/meshcore/repeaters`.
- **Repeater neighbours list is now clickable.** The Health card's "Neighbours" count opens a modal listing each reported neighbour (pubkey prefix, freshest-first by time since last heard, SNR), with names resolved against the known node roster where a pubkey prefix already matches — one batch query across all repeaters, not per-neighbour. A neighbour with a resolved name opens the standard node drawer on click.
- **Repeater card drops the redundant "polled Xm ago" footer.** The Repeaters summary bar already has an "Oldest poll" stat; the identical per-card line was pure duplication once there's only one repeater configured.
- **Live repeater neighbour polls now feed the roster, and each repeater card shows its own "Farthest neighbour."** Previously this data only ever reached `repeater_status.json` (map/neighbour-modal display), never the database — `scripts/import_contacts.py`'s manual `neighbours.json` import was the only way any of this ever reached the `nodes`/`packets` tables. Each poll now also creates/refreshes a placeholder node per reported neighbour (name unknown pubkeys, never overwrites an already-known name/role/position) and a synthetic `nb:<repeater_key>:<node_id>:<timestamp>` packet — same tagging convention as the manual import, just live and attributed to the specific repeater that reported it. `last_heard` only ever moves forward relative to a genuinely-captured packet (a stale secondhand report can never un-freshen a node heard more recently some other way), and nothing here inflates `packet_count` — it's not a packet Meshpoint's own radio received. The Repeaters page's Health card gains a **Farthest neighbour** row (distance, SNR, name) per repeater — measured from *that repeater's own position*, not Meshpoint's, since a polled repeater can be a remote site with a completely different local RF picture. These `nb:`-tagged rows are excluded from the Stats page's own "Farthest Direct Signal" (see the fix above), keeping the two concepts cleanly separated: what Meshpoint itself heard vs. what a repeater it operates heard.
- **Repeater polling gets a dashboard config page.** `repeater_poll:` was the last config section with actual secrets (repeater login passwords) that could only be set by hand-editing `local.yaml`. New **Configuration → Repeater Poll** page: enable/disable, poll interval, and add/rename/remove repeaters (up to 8) from the dashboard. Passwords follow the same convention as the MQTT broker password field — the API only ever reports whether one is *set*, never the value; leave the field blank when editing a repeater to keep its current password. New `PUT /api/config/repeater-poll`, and `GET /api/config` now includes a redacted `repeater_poll` summary. Changes require a restart to take effect, same as the other peripheral/capture-source config pages.
- **MeshCore packet feed no longer buried under bulk-imported telemetry history.** `scripts/import_meshcore_db.py`'s historical telemetry/status import intentionally writes one packet row per sensor channel (not a bug — a repeater's real LPP telemetry snapshot legitimately spans 10-20+ distinct channel/status fields), which meant every historical poll timestamp exploded into a wall of near-identical-looking `telemetry` rows in `GET /api/meshcore/packets`, drowning out genuinely recent mesh activity. That endpoint now excludes `capture_source='meshcore_db_import'` rows by default (`?include_imported=true` still exposes them if ever needed) — the underlying data isn't lost, it's just not the right thing to show in a "what's happening right now" feed; the repeater's own History/Sensors/Trends cards (powered by the separate `telemetry` table) are unaffected either way. Also added two maintenance scripts: `scripts/dedupe_meshcoredb_packets.py` (removes exact `packet_id` duplicates, dry-run by default) and `scripts/purge_meshcoredb_packets.py` (removes the telemetry/status clutter rows entirely, deliberately leaving `meshcoredb:neighbour:%` rows alone since the Topology page's graph query actively depends on them for historical neighbour-star edges).
- **Repeater login no longer gets permanently stuck on a stale route.** User report: a repeater that had been polling fine for a long time started failing every login attempt ("login failed or timed out") continuously — password confirmed correct (a separate BLE-connected tool logged into the same repeater successfully throughout), reception of everything else over that same USB companion kept working normally, and a full Pi reboot didn't help either, ruling out a wrong password or a wedged local session. A directed login is routed over the contact's cached `out_path` in the underlying `meshcore` library; if the mesh topology shifts after that path was learned (a relay it went through reboots, moves, or drops out), every future login keeps retrying the same dead route and times out identically forever — invisible to passive/flood-routed traffic (adverts, messages) since those don't depend on a stored path at all, and untouched by a Meshpoint-side reboot since the stale path is cached state, not a live connection. `poll_repeater()` (`src/transmit/meshcore_tx_client.py`) now calls the library's own `reset_path()` whenever a login fails, clearing the cached path so the very next retry (or next poll round) falls back to flood routing and can learn a fresh one; best-effort and silent on its own failure so it never masks the real login error being reported. **Follow-up fix, same day**: the first version of this fix shipped a bug that made it a no-op — `reset_path()` was called with the short 6-byte contact-lookup prefix (`key`), but the library's destination validation requires a full 32-byte public key (or a contact object carrying one) and raises `ValueError` on anything shorter; the broad `except Exception` around the reset call silently swallowed that, so the path was never actually reset and the live incident this was built for kept failing identically after deploying the "fix." Corrected to pass the already-resolved `contact` object (which carries the full `public_key`) instead of the bare prefix string. **Second follow-up fix, same day**: the corrected reset still wasn't covering every failure shape — it only ran inside the explicit `login is None` branch, but a `wait_for()` timing out anywhere in the login/status/telemetry/neighbours sequence (including login's own wait) raises `asyncio.TimeoutError` past that check entirely, landing in the function's outer exception handlers (`out["error"] = "timed out"`) where no reset ever ran. Moved the reset into the function's `finally` block, gated on any non-empty `out["error"]`, so it now fires uniformly regardless of which specific step or timeout produced the failure. **Diagnostic follow-up, same day**: live logs confirmed the reset now runs successfully on every failed attempt (no exception) but the underlying repeater still times out on every retry regardless — meaning a stale cached path alone doesn't fully explain this specific incident, or the reset isn't landing as expected on the companion device. The reset call's own result wasn't being inspected, only whether it raised, so there was no visibility into what the companion actually replied. Now logs the device's own response event (`OK`/`ERROR`/etc, same pattern already used for `send_advert`) alongside the existing "reset cached path" line, giving a concrete next signal to look at.

#### Self-update system

- **Dashboard update fetch fix.** v0.7.6 added `-c safe.directory` to every sudo git call, which no longer matched the exact-argv NOPASSWD sudoers rules — Check for updates failed with "sudo: a terminal is required". The sudoers file now enumerates the prefixed forms as well.
- **safe.directory migration.** `post_update.sh` registers `/opt/meshpoint` in the system git `safe.directory` on upgraded boxes (previously only fresh installs got it).
- **Channel picker trimmed to this fork.** Release channels are now Stable (main) and Custom branch; upstream's RC and WisMesh entries (branches that do not exist on javastraat/meshpoint) are gone, and previously stored picker ids fall back to Stable.
- **Fork update source.** Version checks and the apply chain point at `javastraat/meshpoint`; git dubious-ownership on the root-owned tree is handled both in-app and at install time.
- **Check for updates shows what's coming.** When the install is behind, the Updates page now lists the incoming commit messages (short SHA + subject, up to 10, "… and N more" beyond that) so you can see what an Apply would bring before pressing it.
- **Latest commits on the Updates page.** The Updates page lists the last five commits on the selected channel's GitHub branch (`origin/main`) — commit date, short SHA, and message — so you can see what happened upstream at a glance; refreshed by Check for updates. Replaces the short-lived apply/rollback history list (and its `GET /api/update/history` endpoint), which only ever showed dashboard button presses, not what changed.
- **Automatic update checks + sidebar pill.** New opt-out `update_check:` config section runs a background task that periodically re-checks for updates — reusing the *exact same* `git fetch` + commits-behind logic as the manual "Check for updates" button (`build_install_status_payload`), so the two never disagree. When an update's found, an "Update available" pill appears right under the device name/status at the very top of the sidebar — the most prominent, always-visible spot, not nested inside anything collapsible; clicking it jumps straight to Settings → Updates. New `GET /api/update/badge` (cheap, cache-only, never triggers a fetch itself) and `PUT /api/update/check-settings`, editable from a new small form on the Updates page. Manually clicking "Check for updates" also refreshes the pill's cache immediately — but only when checking the actual installed channel (compared against the install's own resolved channel, not just "was a channel_id sent at all" — the dashboard always sends one), not a different one from the picker, so trying an alternate branch out of curiosity can't make the pill misreport the real install's status. Applying an update or rolling back re-runs that same check server-side right after success (not just a frontend poke — the backend cache itself is stale otherwise, since neither action previously touched it at all), so the pill clears promptly instead of sitting stuck until the next scheduled interval tick, sometimes an hour later. Interval floored at 5 minutes (each check is a real `git fetch`, not a cheap request).
- **Release notes grouped by category.** The "What's new" preview on the Updates page now shows the changelog's category headings (LoRaWAN sniffing, Roles and access, …) between the bullets instead of one flat list; the `›` bullet marker no longer renders on its own line above each headline.
- **Read full release notes.** The "What's new" preview truncates each bullet to a short teaser; a "Read full release notes" link now opens a modal with the installed version's bullets in full, grouped by category. Served locally (the `release_notes` endpoint returns the full section alongside the preview), so it works on offline gateways.
- **Update check works on dev checkouts.** Git commands for Check for updates only use sudo when the install tree is owned by another user (the Pi's root-owned `/opt/meshpoint`); a checkout owned by the current user runs plain git, so development instances no longer fail with "sudo: a terminal is required to read the password".
- **No more stale-JS breakage after an update.** Applying an update could leave the browser running old cached dashboard JS against the new HTML — features died silently with no console errors until a manual "Empty Cache and Hard Reload". The dashboard page now stamps every local JS/CSS URL with a per-boot `?v=` token (minted at service start, and every apply restarts the service), so browsers refetch fresh assets after each deploy automatically.
- **The service user now owns the whole install tree.** The fan-control fix chowned only the top of `/opt/meshpoint` to the service user, which flipped the sudo auto-detection above into running plain git against the still-root-owned `.git` — Check for updates failed with "cannot open '.git/FETCH_HEAD': Permission denied". Fixed with permissions, recursively: `install.sh`, the systemd unit (every start), and `post_update.sh` (every dashboard apply) all `chown -R` the entire tree to `meshpoint`, so the root-owned files that the apply chain's `sudo git fetch/reset` leaves behind are handed back before the next update check. The sudo auto-detection also probes `.git` (the directory fetch actually writes to) instead of the repo top, so it picks the right mode in mixed-ownership states.
- **Self-update now points at whatever fork you actually cloned, not a hardcoded maintainer's repo.** The version-check and raw-file URLs were hardcoded to `javastraat/meshpoint`; a user running their own fork had no way to redirect them short of editing source. New `src/remote/repo_source.py` reads the `origin` remote straight out of `.git/config` (no `git` subprocess) and derives `owner/repo` from it — a fork's self-update targets itself automatically, with zero configuration. Falls back to the upstream `KMX415/meshpoint` project (not any particular fork) when origin can't be parsed (missing remote, non-GitHub host, unreadable config). The Updates page's "Upstream" card now shows and links to the actual resolved repo instead of the generic `origin/<branch>` label. New `GET /api/update/branches` (admin-only, GitHub API, 5-minute cache) lists the resolved repo's real branches, so the "Custom branch" field now offers them as autocomplete suggestions instead of requiring the exact name typed blind.
#### Backup and restore

- **Settings → System backup and restore.** Download a timestamped `.tar.gz` of `config/local.yaml` and the full `data/` directory (SQLite hot snapshot, PKI keys, rollback state). Restore uploads a prior archive, stashes current state, clears the live `data/` tree, and copies the backup so you return to the snapshot even after **Clear database** or other changes. Each restore runs in its own transient systemd unit so repeat restores work. Archive is not encrypted: store offline and keep it private.
- **Disaster recovery docs.** `TROUBLESHOOTING.md`, `CONFIGURATION.md`, and `COMMON-ERRORS.md` document the fresh-install path (`meshpoint setup` before the dashboard loads), off-Pi backup storage, SSH `restore_finish.sh` fallback, and upstream `HTTP 403` when a revoked API key is restored from backup.

#### Mesh broadcast cadence

- **Position and telemetry interval controls.** Configuration → Radio adds telemetry broadcast interval editor with live countdown. Configuration → GPS adds position broadcast interval editor. Each is independent from NodeInfo: set `interval_minutes` to `0` to pause, or pick 5 min to 24 hr with hot-reload (no restart). Closes [#92](https://github.com/KMX415/meshpoint/issues/92).

#### Dashboard and operator tools

- **RF Environment tab.** Spectral scan and noise-floor telemetry for concentrators with SX1261 spectral-scan support. (On this fork the SenseCap M1 *does* support scan -- set `radio.sx1261_spi_path: "/dev/spidev0.1"`; the tab shares the same scan service as the Band Spectrum card.)
- **RF tab histogram no longer grows the page without bound.** The channel-histogram chart lacked a height-constrained container, so Chart.js re-sized itself into an ever-taller page on hardware that actually produces scan data; the wrapper now has a fixed height.
- **Chart.js vendored locally.** The RF Environment histogram and node-drawer metrics charts loaded Chart.js from a public CDN, so gateways with no outbound internet (offline/air-gapped, mesh-only deployments) silently lost those charts. Now served from `frontend/vendor/chartjs/` alongside the existing vendored xterm.js and qrcode.js, same rationale.
- **Thermals card on the Hardware page.** Six hours of CPU temperature and fan duty history as two stacked time charts sharing the time window (one honest scale per panel, not a dual-axis chart), with hover readouts and a live "temp · fan %" header. Backed by new `GET /api/device/thermals`, fed from an in-memory ring buffer sampled by the fan controller's poll loop — no database, cleared on restart. Only appears when fan control is enabled, like the stat-bar Fan card.
- **Operator status strips.** KPI-style strips on Dashboard and RF tabs; MQTT broker health on Configuration → MQTT.
- **Quick Deploy QR.** Configuration → Channels exports public channel parameters as a scannable QR for field provisioning.
- **Prometheus `/metrics`.** Optional scrape endpoint with packet, node, relay, and system counters.
- **Channel hash map refresh.** Rebuild Meshtastic channel hashes after dashboard channel save so MQTT topics and decoders stay aligned. Fixes [#89](https://github.com/KMX415/meshpoint/issues/89).
- **Terminal quick-command: "Run install.sh (upgrade software)".** The dashboard's "Apply update" (git pull + restart) intentionally skips the full installer to stay fast, so a release adding a new system dependency (e.g. `welle.io` for DAB+) previously needed an SSH session to install it -- users had no way to discover that step existed. New `Setup`-category entry in the Terminal tab's command catalog inserts `sudo /bin/bash /opt/meshpoint/scripts/install.sh` at the prompt (marked `dangerous`, same confirm-before-insert treatment as restarting the service); the Terminal itself is a full PTY already, so no new execution machinery was needed, just a discoverable button. Fixed same day: the command initially read `cd /opt/meshpoint && sudo bash scripts/install.sh`, which prompted for a password the `meshpoint` service account doesn't have -- `config/sudoers-meshpoint` only grants NOPASSWD for the exact absolute-path invocation (`/bin/bash /opt/meshpoint/scripts/install.sh`, no wildcards on the binary/script path), and sudo does strict argv matching, so the relative-path form silently fell through to an interactive prompt instead of matching the grant. Fixed a second, more subtle bug the same day: running `install.sh` from the web Terminal (but not from a real SSH shell) could stop partway through. Root cause: `scripts/patch_hal.sh`, called mid-`install.sh` during the HAL compile step, prints "Done. Restart meshpoint: sudo systemctl restart meshpoint" -- correct advice when that script is run standalone, but premature when it's a substep of `install.sh`, which still has several sections left to run (sudoers, systemd service, watchdog, CLI tools) before its own correctly-timed final banner. Acting on that premature suggestion restarts the meshpoint service mid-install, and since the web Terminal's PTY is a child process inside meshpoint's own systemd cgroup (unlike an independent SSH session), the restart kills the PTY -- and the rest of the install run -- before it finishes; a real SSH shell is untouched by the same restart, which is why the problem only showed up in the dashboard. Fixed by a new `MESHPOINT_INSTALL_IN_PROGRESS` env var that `install.sh` (and `apply_finish.sh`, whose own `post_update.sh` migrations can also trigger the HAL patch) set before calling `patch_hal.sh`, telling it to skip the premature suggestion since the caller already prints its own restart prompt (or, for `apply_finish.sh`, already restarts automatically right after). **Removed 2026-07-20**: even with that fix, running this command from the web Terminal still kills the terminal's own PTY session at the very end -- install.sh's own correctly-timed final restart of the `meshpoint` service takes the web Terminal down with it, since that PTY lives inside the very service being restarted (a real SSH shell doesn't have this problem). User: "that doesnt work because it kills the terminal" -- removed the quick-command button entirely rather than leave a one-click action in the dashboard that reliably cuts its own session; running `install.sh` is still fully supported from a real SSH/CLI session, just no longer one click away from the Terminal tab. Removing it left the `Setup` category empty, so that category was dropped too.
- **Terminal quick-commands: 3 new DAB+ scan entries.** New `DAB+`-category entries in the Terminal tab's command catalog (`src/api/terminal/command_catalog.py`) insert `scripts/dab_channel_scan.py` at the prompt in three common shapes: a full 38-channel scan at the default timeout, the same full scan with a longer 60s/channel timeout for a weaker antenna, and a targeted 60s rescan of just the 5 channels already confirmed live at this antenna (`7D 8B 9C 11C 12C`) -- much faster than a full scan when the goal is just fresh station lists. Not marked `dangerous` (the script is a non-destructive read-only scan that only writes its own results file), but the description text calls out that another running Radio/DAB+/P2000/Pagers/POCSAG/RTL433 tab should be stopped first, since this script drives `welle-cli` directly and has no awareness of the dashboard's own dongle-exclusivity lock.

#### Docs

**Sidebar: real Meshtastic/MeshCore brand icons + Topology icon swap, 2026-08-02.** User asked whether Meshtastic/MeshCore's actual logos could replace the sidebar's generic line-icons, starting from a `favicon.ico` idea. Investigated both projects' real repos before touching anything (WebSearch/WebFetch, not guessed):

- **Meshtastic**: has a formal trademark policy (`meshtastic.org/docs/legal/licensing-and-trademark/`) — using the main logo without permission is a grey area, but the project publishes an official **"M-Powered" badge** (`meshtastic/design`, `Meshtastic Powered Logo/M-PWRD.svg`) specifically for third-party compatibility marks, explicitly not requiring a trademark grant. Used that instead of the primary logo.
- **MeshCore**: MIT-licensed end to end (`meshcore-dev/MeshCore`), `logo/meshcore.svg` in the repo, no separate trademark carve-out found. Low risk. Only publishes a horizontal wordmark though, no square icon-mark — so rather than force the whole wordmark into the 18px icon slot, just the "M" (the wordmark's first `<path>`, own tight viewBox) was lifted out and used with `fill="currentColor"`.
- **The Things Network** (asked separately, for the LoRaWAN icon): official assets at `thethingsnetwork.org/brand-assets/` include a circular mark (icon + spelled-out wordmark) under looser "non-commercial + comply with our manifest" terms. The wordmark text is illegible at 18px like MeshCore's; the enclosed blue network/cloud icon graphic was croppable on its own (bounding-box computed via a small Python path-parser, not eyeballed) but **rejected after live preview** — at icon size it just reads as a generic cloud, not distinctly TTN-branded, less clear than the existing signal-ripple icon it would have replaced. **LoRaWAN's icon was left unchanged** per user's explicit call after seeing it live.

**Design/preview process**: built an interactive Artifact (real sidebar CSS tokens copied from `sidebar.css`/`dashboard.css` — dark bg `#0d1422`, 18px icon slot, exact hover/active states) with clickable rows so the user could see the actual active/inactive states before any code changed, rather than describing it in prose. Iterated twice on the TTN crop live in the preview: first attempt used the source SVG's native wide aspect ratio (540×255), which under default `preserveAspectRatio="xMidYMid meet"` shrank to fill only the 18px slot's width, rendering at ~8px tall inside the square slot — user reported "half a circle" (a squished, unrecognizable blob). Fixed by recomputing a **square, centered viewBox** (same shape, no distortion, just more surrounding empty space) so it renders at the full 18px like the other icons — technically correct after that, but still visually rejected on its own merits per above.

**Landed design**: Meshtastic's badge is a **fixed-palette SVG** (navy/green/white baked in from Meshtastic's own brand colors), not `currentColor` — so it can't just inherit the sidebar's muted/active tokens the way every other icon does. Solved with a CSS filter toggle instead of a recolor: `.sidebar__icon--badge-mt svg { filter: grayscale(1) opacity(0.5); }` normally, `filter: none` under `.sidebar__link[aria-current="page"] .sidebar__icon--badge-mt svg` — grey when not the active route, full brand color (including its own green) when it is. MeshCore's isolated "M" needed no such treatment since it's a real `fill="currentColor"` line-icon now, same mechanism as every other nav icon.

**Implementation** (`frontend/index.html`, `frontend/sidebar/sidebar.css`): both icons inlined directly as `<svg>` markup in the sidebar nav list, matching how every other icon in this file is already authored (no separate asset files, no `<img>`/`<use>` indirection — consistent with the existing all-inline convention). Each carries an HTML comment citing its exact source file and the trademark/license reasoning above, so a future reader doesn't have to redo this research. **Bonus, same session**: user pointed out the freed-up old MeshCore icon (triangle point-up: circle top-center + two circles bottom corners) was a nicer shape than Topology's existing icon (triangle point-down: two circles top + one bottom) — swapped Topology onto the old MeshCore glyph verbatim.

**Verification**: `tests/test_html_assets.py` 7/7; `docs/CHANGELOG.md` re-parses via the real `ChangelogParser.parse_file()` (`src/api/update/release_notes.py`) at 27 sections; changelog bullet added under `### v0.7.9` (confirmed via `src/version.py` that 0.7.9, not 0.7.7, is now the live section — the CLAUDE.md "v0.7.7 while it lasts" note is stale, follow `src/version.py` as the source of truth going forward). SVG tag-balance and `cls-mt1/2/3` class-name-uniqueness sanity-checked via grep. **Not yet live-viewed on the Pi** — next visit should confirm the grayscale↔color transition and the M/Topology-triangle swap render as intended in the real browser, not just the standalone Artifact preview.

Chose not to fix this now: a proper fix means actually renaming the route to `settings/advanced` end-to-end (nav link, the `data-section="configuration/advanced"` content wrapper, `allowedRoutes`, the guard's `requiredSection()`, `ConfigurationPanel`'s dispatch match, AND the backend's hardcoded `"configuration.advanced"` string in `identity_routes.py`) -- real backend-touching work, disproportionate for something the user already called out as temporary pending the later real card-split. **Storage page rename completed properly: settings/storage route + settings.storage permission key, 2026-08-02 (same session, immediate follow-on).** After the label-only rename (previous entry), user asked point-blank whether the route should also say "storage" instead of "advanced" -- caught that my earlier choice to keep `configuration/advanced` unrenamed was pure low-effort convenience (reusing the guard's generic `configuration/X -> configuration.X` rule), not a principled decision. Answered honestly (my `configuration/` choice was effort-driven, not correctness-driven) and recommended going all the way, citing the exact existing precedent already in the code: `settings/dangerous` already gets its own specific permission key via a special-cased guard line rather than falling into the generic `settings` bucket -- Storage could get identical treatment. User agreed ("yes please for consistancy").

**Full implementation, `configuration/storage` -> `settings/storage` end to end**:
- `frontend/index.html`: sidebar link href/data-route -> `settings/storage`; the lazy-load section wrapper's `data-section` -> `settings/storage` and its div id `cfg-storage-panel` -> `settings-storage-panel` (matching the naming convention already used by the other genuine Settings pages, confirmed by checking `settings-updates-panel`/`settings-auth-panel`/`settings-dangerous-panel` first rather than guessing); the whole `<section>` block physically relocated from among the `configuration/*` section wrappers to sit with the other `settings/*` blocks, for a reader-facing tidiness, not just correctness (functionally the DOM position never mattered -- `_renderActive()` matches by attribute, not position -- but a future reader scanning for Settings pages shouldn't have to know Storage is hiding in the Configuration block).
- `frontend/js/app.js`: moved `'configuration/storage'` out of the allowedRoutes' configuration group into the settings group as `'settings/storage'`; added `if (route === 'settings/storage') return 'settings.storage';` to `_buildRouteGuard()`'s `requiredSection()`, positioned right after the existing `settings/dangerous` special case and before the generic `settings/` bucket fallback -- exact same pattern, not a new one invented.
- `frontend/js/configuration/configuration_panel.js`: `onSectionEnter(route)` special-cases `route === 'settings/storage'` (in addition to the generic `configuration/` prefix check) since Storage's mounting logic stays centralized on this panel rather than needing a whole new dedicated controller for one card; `_mountSection`'s storage branch host lookup updated to the new `settings-storage-panel` id.
- `src/api/routes/identity_routes.py`: **caught by the user mid-edit, not by me** -- "make sure we dont get this admin required popup we are admin" -- the `_ADMIN_SECTIONS` tuple still had the OLD `"configuration.storage"` string from the prior intermediate rename step; if left stale, admin's `available_sections` would no longer contain whatever key the frontend guard actually derives (`settings.storage`), and even the admin role would get denied/toasted "Admin access required" on a route that should obviously be allowed. Fixed: `"configuration.storage"` removed, `"settings.storage"` added (positioned with the other `settings.*` entries). This is exactly the kind of two-sided (frontend route derives a permission STRING; backend must independently grant that SAME STRING) consistency bug that's easy to half-fix -- worth remembering for any future route/permission rename: the frontend guard and the backend's per-role section list are two separate hardcoded sources of truth that must be updated together, there's no single shared enum.
- `storage_card.js` docstring updated to describe the final `settings/storage`/`settings.storage` naming instead of the superseded intermediate `configuration/storage` one.

**Verification**: `node --check` clean on all 4 touched JS files; `ast.parse` clean on `identity_routes.py`; grep confirmed zero residual `configuration/storage`/`configuration.storage`/`cfg-storage-panel` references anywhere (the one remaining "configuration" hit is `js/configuration/storage_card.js`'s script *path*, which is just the file's directory location on disk, unrelated to its route -- `radio_advanced_card.js` lives in the same directory despite being part of Configuration → Radio, so this isn't a real inconsistency); grep confirmed all 8 expected `settings/storage`/`settings.storage`/`settings-storage-panel` references are present in exactly the right files; `tests/test_html_assets.py` 7/7; changelog bullet under `v0.7.9` updated to describe the final state rather than the superseded intermediate one (27 sections). **Not yet live-tested** -- next Pi visit is the first real chance to confirm the admin role actually reaches Settings → Storage without the "Admin access required" toast the user was specifically worried about, since the permission-string plumbing can only be fully verified against a real logged-in session with real JWT claims, not from the Mac.

**Fixed malformed SVG path data across 3 icons, 2026-08-02 (same session, live-debugging the Settings -> Storage blank-page report).** While chasing why Settings -> Storage rendered stuck on "Loading..." live on the Pi (routing/permission/sidebar all confirmed working via a fresh incognito test -- ruled out browser cache), user pasted a browser console error: `<path> attribute d: Expected number, "....840996683957201Z"`. Traced it to a real, separate bug: the Meshtastic M-Powered badge SVG (added earlier this session, sourced from Meshtastic's own official Illustrator export) has several `<path>` elements where two adjacent decimal numbers collide with no separator (e.g. `.572578386265377.818731742230739`, ambiguous/invalid per SVG number grammar -- a sign can implicitly separate two numbers but a second `.` cannot). Wrote a small Python script to programmatically scan every `d="..."` attribute in `index.html` for this exact collision pattern (`\.\d+\.\d+`) rather than eyeballing thousands of characters, which turned up the SAME defect in two more places: the base-station Repeaters icon (also user-supplied this session) and, unexpectedly, the pre-existing Settings gear icon (original app code, never touched this session, presumably always had this defect silently).

Fixed with a safe, semantically-neutral global substitution (insert a comma between the two colliding number tokens -- never changes the rendered shape, just disambiguates parsing), applied iteratively per attribute since some collisions were 3+ numbers deep (a single non-overlapping regex pass left some residual collisions on the first attempt, caught by re-scanning after and looping until stable). Verified via two independent full-file rescans showing zero remaining collisions, and confirmed via `git diff --stat` that exactly 8 lines were touched (6 in the Meshtastic badge, 1 repeater icon, 1 gear icon) -- matches expectation exactly, nothing touched outside the known-affected paths.

**Important finding communicated to the user**: this SVG bug is very unlikely to be the actual cause of the Settings -> Storage blank page. A malformed `<path>` `d` attribute is a browser rendering-layer warning, not a JavaScript exception -- it cannot halt or block unrelated `<script>` tag execution elsewhere in the document. The two issues (broken SVG rendering, blank Storage card content) are almost certainly independent bugs that both happened to be visible in the same debugging session. **The real Storage-page root cause is still open** -- asked the user to check DevTools -> Network tab (not Console) specifically for `storage_card.js`'s HTTP status, to confirm or rule out the leading hypothesis (a deploy/sync gap -- this session's file rename from `advanced_card.js` to `storage_card.js` may not have propagated to whatever serves the live Pi yet, since nothing this session has been committed/pushed through normal git channels). Not yet resolved as of this entry.

**Settings -> Storage blank-page bug: root cause found and fixed, 2026-08-02 (same session, resolves the long live-debugging thread).** Root cause: `frontend/js/app.js`'s `_bootConfigurationPanel(router)` has its OWN, separate, duplicate route-prefix guard at the subscription level -- `router.onRouteChange((route) => { if (!route || !route.startsWith('configuration/')) return; panel.onSectionEnter(route); })` -- which I completely missed when adding the `isStorage` special case to `ConfigurationPanel.onSectionEnter()` itself. Since `'settings/storage'` doesn't start with `'configuration/'`, this OUTER wrapper silently returned before ever calling `panel.onSectionEnter()` -- the method never ran for real traffic, while every diagnostic I asked the user to run in the console (`new ConfigurationPanel().onSectionEnter('settings/storage')`, manually calling `StorageConfigCard.mount()` directly) bypassed this wrapper entirely and worked perfectly, which is exactly why every individual piece checked out healthy (`typeof StorageConfigCard === 'function'`, `typeof ConfigurationPanel === 'function'`, correct DOM id, correct route string, no thrown errors, no unhandled rejections) while the real page stayed stuck.

**How it was found**: exhausted static reading and indirect testing first (title/route/permission/DOM id all individually verified via live console commands run by the user against the actual deployed Pi, since neither of us could reproduce the exact live JS execution context any other way) -- when those all came back clean, added TEMPORARY `console.log` trace statements directly into `onSectionEnter` (route received, computed section, `_mounted` state, post-mount innerHTML) to force the next reload to reveal ground truth rather than continuing to guess. While re-reading `app.js` to also expose the real panel instance on `window` for a `this === realInstance` comparison (part of setting up that trace), spotted the actual duplicate guard sitting right there in `_bootConfigurationPanel` -- found it by re-reading the surrounding code with fresh eyes while wiring the debug aid, not from the trace output itself (never had to ship the debug build). Removed the temp logging immediately once the real fix was identified rather than leaving debug noise in.

**Fix**: `_bootConfigurationPanel`'s guard updated to also allow `route === 'settings/storage'` through, mirroring the `isStorage` special case already added to `ConfigurationPanel.onSectionEnter()` itself -- the two checks now agree. **Lesson for next time a route gets a similar cross-boundary exception** (a page whose content-mounting logic stays on one controller while its route lives under a different top-level prefix): grep for EVERY place that checks the route prefix, not just the "obvious" one inside the class method itself -- `app.js`'s subscription-site guard was easy to miss because it duplicates logic that conceptually "belongs" to `ConfigurationPanel`, sitting one abstraction layer higher in a different file.

**Known, non-blocking follow-up NOT fixed today**: `_mountSection()` unconditionally calls `this._mounted.add(section)` at the very end of the method regardless of whether any if-else branch actually matched -- a genuine latent bug (a future typo'd/unmatched section would get silently marked "already mounted" forever, exactly mimicking today's symptom) that happened to NOT be the cause this time (today's bug was the call never reaching `_mountSection` at all) but is still worth hardening later: only mark a section mounted when a branch actually ran.

Verified: `node --check` clean on both touched files; `tests/test_html_assets.py` 7/7; changelog bullet under `v0.7.9` (27 sections). **Still needs live confirmation** -- next Pi visit/redeploy should show Settings -> Storage actually populating on a real fresh load, closing out this whole debugging thread for good.

**PLANNING ONLY, NOT YET STARTED — concentrator idle-capacity brainstorm + Pager project scoped, 2026-08-02 (same session, end of day).** Originated from the user's weekly "hackers hangout" — a fun brainstorm of ideas for the concentrator's unused capacity, several evaluated together and most explicitly *not* pursued:

**Ideas raised and their verdict:**
- **Pager system** — the one actually being built. See below.
- **"Kermit telephone" (old analog-phone-style idea) using Codec2** — user's own hangout already concluded "not working," confirmed why: LoRa is packetized and largely half-duplex with real airtime/duty-cycle limits; even Codec2's ~700-1200bps voice can't get a continuous, low-latency phone-call-like stream out of that. Not pursued.
- **Voice PTT repeater** (phone-BLE-Heltec-868-Heltec-BLE-phone) — flagged as the most technically credible of the "fun" ideas, NOT the telephone idea's dead end, because push-to-talk is inherently bursty/half-duplex — the same shape LoRa is actually good at. Codec2 runs fine on ESP32, BLE audio bridge to phone is well-trodden. **Candidate second project after the pager**, not started.
- **Silent disco** — two different ideas under one label. *Listening in* is an RTL-SDR job (already have that tab), not a concentrator-channel thing — silent discos run their own dedicated transmitters, not on meshpoint's LoRa channels. *Transmitting into* someone else's event is the "questionable" one the user flagged themselves — real RF interference into someone else's system without consent. Advised against; not pursued.
- **Wireless microphone** — same wall as the telephone idea, worse (continuous audio, not even PTT bursts). Doesn't fit LoRa's channel-access model. Not pursued.

**Concentrator idle-capacity ground truth** (verified via a research subagent reading the real code, not guessed — src/hal/concentrator_config.py, src/hal/sx1302_wrapper.py, src/hal/sx1302_types.py, docs/BANDPLAN.md):
- `LGW_IF_CHAIN_NB = 10` total IF chains; Meshpoint's `eu868_lorawan()` plan (the real deployed EU868 profile — 5 TTN LoRaWAN uplinks on RF0 + Meshtastic on ch8/RF1) only populates 9 of them.
- **ch5-ch7**: 3 disabled multi-SF LoRa IF chains, anchored at 869.525 MHz on RF1 (same physical chain as Meshtastic LongFast) — `concentrator_config.py:200-203`, comment: "nothing LoRaWAN-useful within ±490 kHz of RF1". These are real, usable **LoRa** demodulators sitting idle, not FSK.
- **ch9** ("channel 10" in the user's 1-based counting): the SX1302's one dedicated **FSK**-capable IF chain. Never configured anywhere in this codebase — confirmed idle by `docs/BANDPLAN.md`'s own comment ("1 FSK channel (not used by Meshpoint)"). No `MOD_FSK` constant exists anywhere in `src/hal/` today (only `MOD_LORA = 0x10`); the real Semtech HAL's FSK-shaped struct fields (e.g. `f_dev` in `LgwPktTxS`) exist but are unused — genuine unimplemented capability, not a hardware limit.
- The SX1302's ±490 kHz digital IF window around RF1's 869.525 MHz anchor comfortably covers the **869.4-869.65 MHz ETSI high-power sub-band** (500 mW/27 dBm, 10% duty cycle) the user specifically asked about — this sub-band needs **zero RF-chain retuning**, since RF1 already sits almost exactly there for Meshtastic.
- TX is hard-gated in code to `rf_chain == 0` (`sx1302_wrapper.py:506`) — but since Meshtastic (on RF1/869.525 MHz) is *already proven transmitting live in production* (per the earlier "concentrator TX sync word fix" milestone), this must mean TX bursts retune chip 0's synthesizer per-packet independent of RF1's nominal RX anchor, not that TX is frequency-limited to near 868.3 MHz — flagged as **still not 100% verified against the real libloragw C source**, just inferred from the fact Meshtastic TX already works at 869.525 MHz through whatever this mechanism actually is.

**Pager project, as actually scoped (implementation NOT started yet, user said "don't do anything yet"):**
- **Not POCSAG.** Corrected a real architecture mix-up mid-conversation: the user initially proposed using "channel 10" (the FSK chain) for a *two-way, send-and-receive* pager — but FSK and LoRa are incompatible modulations on the same slot; a Heltec V3 + RadioLib doing send/receive natively speaks LoRa. FSK/ch9 only matters for real POCSAG/DAPNET compatibility, which the user explicitly said is *not* the goal here ("no not pocsag realy using the most out of the concentrator :)") — the actual goal is fuller utilization of otherwise-idle capacity, not protocol compatibility with anything external.
- **Correct channel pick: one of ch5-ch7** (plain LoRa, already covered by RF1's existing 869.4-869.65 MHz window, no retuning needed), given its own **distinct sync word** — same trick already used to keep LoRaWAN (0x34) and Meshtastic (0x2B) apart on shared hardware (`sx1302_wrapper.py`'s `set_syncword`/`set_tx_syncword`) — so pager traffic stays fully separate from regular mesh routing/relay instead of mixing into it, while reusing the exact TX/RX mechanism already proven working for Meshtastic (not new FSK engineering).
- **Dashboard**: a new dedicated **Pager** page (sidebar item, matching the existing per-protocol pattern — LoRaWAN/Meshtastic/MeshCore/DAPNET each already get their own page), with **send and receive** UI.
- **Receiver/sender hardware**: **Heltec V3** (user already owns several, buying a few more) — confirmed same SX1262 radio + ESP32-S3 core as the newer Heltec V4, so firmware written for one runs unchanged on the other; V4 was investigated (WebSearch: <20µA sleep current, built-in PC casing + integrated antenna, solar charging interface, pin-compatible with V3) as a strong option for future *pager-specific* purchases given its better standby power and ready-made wearable-friendly casing, but not needed to start — V3 is fine and already on hand.
- **Firmware design, corrected from the original one-way-broadcast framing to two-way**: RadioLib in native LoRa mode (no FSK bit-banging needed at all, genuinely simpler than `pocsag_companion.ino`'s FSK decoder) — same general Arduino+RadioLib+OLED pattern already proven via `pocsag_companion.ino` and the arduino-cli compile/flash toolchain already built into the dashboard this session (reusable directly for this new sketch), but must both send AND receive, unlike the original one-way-alert concept. Own distinct sync word (matching the channel choice above) so it never picks up regular Meshtastic mesh chatter.
- **The idle FSK chain (ch9) is explicitly untouched by this project** and remains available for a genuinely different future idea (real POCSAG/DAPNET compatibility, or something else FSK-shaped) — nothing about building the pager on ch5-7 uses up that capacity.

**Pager brainstorm continued: channel-isolation approach picked, button UX sketched, 2026-08-02 (same session, still pure planning, nothing built).**

**Channel-wise approach for ch5-7 isolation, decided (option A of three brainstormed)**: extend the existing `set_syncword()`/`set_tx_syncword()` direct-register-write mechanism (currently only implemented for ch8, Meshtastic's service channel) to also cover one of the multi-SF slots (ch5-7), giving the pager channel its own distinct sync word instead of inheriting LoRaWAN's public `0x34` (which is what `lorawan_public=True` sets uniformly across ch0-ch7 at `lgw_start()`, confirmed via `sx1302_wrapper.py:485` -- there's no existing per-channel override for the multi-SF slots, only ch8 got that treatment). This was weighed against two cheaper alternatives before picking A: (B) leave it on LoRaWAN's 0x34 and filter by a magic byte in the payload instead (zero new HAL work, but leaks pager traffic to real nearby LoRaWAN gateways and exposes the pager to real LoRaWAN noise); (C) skip a new IF chain entirely and just add the pager as another named/PSK'd Meshtastic channel on the already-proven ch8 (zero concentrator-side work, but needs the pager firmware to speak real Meshtastic protobuf+AES-CCM instead of a small custom format). User picked A specifically for genuine interference-free isolation from both Meshtastic and LoRaWAN traffic -- known to be the one option needing real new register-level engineering (the SX1302 register offsets for an arbitrary multi-SF IF chain haven't been reverse-engineered the way ch8's were), a one-time cost accepted knowingly.

**Hardware confirmed**: standard/stock Heltec V3 enclosure, no custom case or extra buttons -- just the board's own PRG (boot) button + reset button, matching the "no free-text input, canned messages only" design already settled on.

**Button UX, sketched as a single-button state machine**:
- **Idle** (default/at-rest state): OLED shows the last received message -- glanceable, no interaction needed, matches how a real pager should behave at rest.
- **Long-hold from idle**: enters the reply menu, starting on the first canned-message option.
- **In menu, short press**: cycles to the next canned option.
- **In menu, long-hold**: sends the currently highlighted option, drops back to idle.

Two refinements flagged for whenever this gets built (not decided yet, just noted so they aren't forgotten): (1) a timeout back to idle if the button goes untouched for a few seconds while in the menu, so it can't get stuck showing a stale menu; (2) whether a new incoming message arriving while someone's mid-menu should interrupt immediately or wait until they exit the menu -- leaning toward "wait," so a message doesn't yank the menu away mid-selection, but genuinely still open.

**Status: still pure brainstorming, nothing built.** Full picture now spans this entry + the previous "concentrator idle-capacity brainstorm + Pager project scoped" entry above -- read both together for the complete plan when this gets picked up for real.

**DAPNET Send tab built: firmware, backend, and frontend, 2026-08-02 (same session, first real implementation after the pager planning arc).** User asked for a way to send POCSAG pages from the dashboard, referencing the serial protocol comment in `pocsag_companion.ino` (`IN: {"text":...}` or `{"capcode":...,"text":...}`). Investigated before building (research subagent): confirmed `DapnetSerialSource` had zero send capability (read-only today), but its generic request/response primitive `send_command()` (matches replies by `"type"` field) already existed and needed no changes -- and found a real gotcha worth solving properly: the companion's serial-triggered send path had **no JSON reply at all**, only plain-text log lines (`"[serial] SENT OK"`/`"SEND FAILED"`/`"SEND BLOCKED"`) that the Python parser silently drops. User explicitly chose the "correct path" (real confirmation) over a fire-and-forget optimistic UI, noting the same reliable-ack pattern will matter again for the 868 MHz pager project later.

**Firmware** (`extra/pocsag_companion/pocsag_companion.ino`): `sendPocsagAlpha()` changed from `void` to returning `String` ("ok"/"blocked"/"failed") -- the BLOCKED early-return and the success/failure branch at the end both now return a result, while every existing `Serial.print`/`pushWebLog`/`showSentScreen` side-effect stays exactly as it was. `handleSerialJsonLine()` (the bare `{"text":...}`/`{"capcode":...,"text":...}` path, no `"cmd"` wrapper -- distinct from the `cmd`-based commands like `status`/`set_callsign`) now captures that result and emits a dedicated `{"type":"send_result","ok":...,"reason":...}` JSON reply, deliberately kept separate from the existing success-only "echo as an alpha page" JSON (which stays exactly as-is, still shaped like a received page so it shows up in Recent Pages for free) -- the echo alone was too ambiguous to build a reliable ack on (a real incoming page from someone else could coincidentally also have `"type":"alpha"` at the same moment, and there was never any reply at all for blocked/failed). The web dashboard's own send path (`checkWebSendPending()`) calls the same now-`String`-returning function but ignores the return value, so its behavior is provably unchanged. **Compile-verified on the Mac** via the same local `arduino-cli` toolchain used earlier this session (`esp32:esp32:heltec_wifi_lora_32_V3`, 1,210,931 bytes / 36%, clean).

**Backend** (`src/api/routes/dapnet_config_routes.py`): new `POST /api/config/dapnet/send` (label/capcode-optional/text), added to the SAME already-mounted router the existing callsign/web-password/reset-credentials/wifi/reboot routes live on -- confirmed via `server.py` that both the router and its `init_routes(dapnet_sources=...)` wiring already existed, so no `server.py` changes were needed at all, just the new endpoint. Calls `source.send_command({"text":...[,"capcode":...]}, expect_type="send_result", timeout=10.0)` -- reusing the exact same generic mechanism the other DAPNET commands use, no new plumbing on `DapnetSerialSource` itself. 10s timeout (not the other commands' 5s) since this one waits for a real over-the-air TX, not an instant NVS write. **Verified with a from-scratch stubbed exercise** (no existing test file covered this module at all before this change) against a fake source object covering all 7 real outcomes: success (bare + with explicit capcode, confirming the capcode key is only added to the outgoing command when given), blocked (400), TX failed (502), timeout/no reply (503), not-connected (503), and empty-text (400) -- all passed on the first correct version (after fixing a missing `.name` attribute on the first draft of the fake source).

**Frontend** (`frontend/js/dapnet_panel.js`): third "Send" tab alongside Recent Pages/Capcodes, reusing the exact same generic `data-dp-tab`/`data-dp-view` tab mechanism (confirmed by the research subagent to need zero changes to `_setTab`/`_applyTab` -- both already generic loops) plus the app's global `cfg-form`/`cfg-field`/`cfg-status`/`terminal-button` classes (confirmed unscoped in `configuration.css`, safe to reuse on a non-Configuration page, and `configuration.css` is already unconditionally loaded in `index.html` regardless of current route) rather than inventing new CSS. Device picker (`_loadSendDevices()`/`_renderSendDevices()`) fetches `/api/config` for `pocsag_serial` (configured labels) + `dapnet_status` (live connected state, matched by the same `dapnet_<label>`/bare `dapnet` naming convention `_resolve_dapnet_source` uses server-side) and only shows the picker when 2+ companions are configured -- same "don't ask when there's nothing to choose between" convention used by the firmware cards earlier this session. Capcode field is optional (omitted from the POST body entirely when blank, letting the companion fall back to its own configured default) rather than sending a placeholder value.

**Verified with a real (not just syntax-checked) exercise**: built a minimal fake DOM in a live Node/V8 context (not jsdom, just enough `FakeElement`/`document.getElementById` stubbing to run the real class unmodified) and confirmed: device-picker hidden with 0 or 1 devices, shown with 2+, correct "(offline)" marker rendering; `_handleSend()` builds the exact right POST body (text trimmed, capcode coerced to a real number, label passed through) via a faked `fetch`, correctly shows "Sent." and clears the text input on success, and correctly shows the server's real error message and leaves the text input untouched on failure. `node --check` clean; `tests/test_html_assets.py` 7/7.

**Docs**: changelog bullet added under the existing `#### DAPNET (POCSAG companion)` subsection (already the natural home, given how many prior DAPNET features already live there), `v0.7.9` section, re-parses at 27 sections.

**Not yet live-tested on real hardware** -- next step when picked back up: flash the updated `pocsag_companion.ino` (via the dashboard's own existing Compile/Flash card, matching how every previous firmware iteration this session got onto the real board) and confirm a Send-tab click actually transmits and the dashboard shows a real "Sent."/error result end to end, not just the stubbed logic paths verified here.

**Real bug found live, same day as the DAPNET Send tab build: wrong config path.** User tested immediately on the real Pi: Send tab showed "POCSAG companion not connected" even though the companion was clearly live (topbar chip green, receiving pages normally, "test" page they sent even echoed in as a received page) -- and confirmed nothing showed in `meshpoint logs` either, which is actually consistent with the bug rather than a separate mystery (the route hits `_resolve_dapnet_source()` and returns a clean, un-logged 503 when it finds no match, not a crash).

**Root cause**: `_loadSendDevices()` read `cfg.pocsag_serial` directly off the top-level `/api/config` response, but the real configured-device list lives nested under `cfg.capture.pocsag_serial` -- confirmed by checking how `pocsag_serial_card.js` (Configuration -> POCSAG's own existing card) actually reads it (`const cap = config.capture || {}; const devices = cap.pocsag_serial`). Never checked this against the real shape before shipping, just assumed a flat top-level key by analogy with `dapnet_status` (which genuinely IS top-level, confirmed separately in `config_routes.py` -- so the two fields have different nesting, an easy assumption to get wrong without checking both). The empty device list meant the Send tab's device `<select>` never got populated, so the label sent with every request didn't match the real device.

Fixed: `cfg.pocsag_serial` -> `(cfg.capture || {}).pocsag_serial`. Re-verified with a stubbed exercise using the REAL nested shape this time (not the wrong flat one the original test happened to use, which is exactly why the original stub test passed despite the bug -- worth remembering: a stub that mirrors your own wrong assumption proves nothing). `node --check` clean, `tests/test_html_assets.py` 7/7, changelog bullet added as a same-day fix under the original Send-tab bullet. User had already reflashed the companion with the new firmware separately, so once this frontend fix is live the whole path should work end to end -- not yet confirmed.

**DAPNET Send tab locked down to admin only, 2026-08-02 (same session, right after confirming the send flow works live).** User asked to hide/block the Send tab for viewers. Investigated first (research subagent): the backend route was ALREADY admin-gated (`require_admin`, same as every other dapnet_config_routes.py command) -- so "reach" was already covered; this was purely about "see" (hiding the tab in the UI for viewers). Found there was NO existing precedent anywhere in this codebase for "one in-page element role-gated while the rest of the page stays viewer-visible" -- the two existing patterns are page-level (`data-requires-section` on sidebar `<li>`s, driven by `identity.available_sections`) or purely reactive (Messages' compose bar has no role-check at all; a viewer can click Send, the API 403s, and `messaging.js` catches that and toasts "Not sent: ..."). Neither fit a tab that should be properly invisible, not just error-on-attempt -- built a new (first-of-its-kind-in-this-app) proactive client-side hide.

**Key plumbing gap found and fixed**: `identity` (fetched once at boot in `app.js`'s `DOMContentLoaded` handler) was never exposed to any page-specific panel class -- only passed into `Router`/`SidebarController`'s constructors. `_bootDapnetPanel(router)` is a hoisted top-level function, so it can't close over `identity` (a local variable inside the async boot callback) even though they're both defined in the same file -- confirmed this was a real gap, not an oversight I could route around, by checking `new window.DapnetPanel()` was called with zero arguments. Fixed narrowly: `_bootDapnetPanel(router, identity)` at the call site, `new window.DapnetPanel(identity)` inside it -- constructor injection, matching how Router/SidebarController already receive identity, not a new `window.identity` global.

**Gating logic** (`DapnetPanel` constructor): `this._isAdmin = identity?.role !== 'viewer'` -- deliberately fails OPEN (undefined identity, or an identity object with no `role` field at all -- the real shape whenever there's no session cookie -- both count as "admin-like"), matching the exact same fail-open philosophy already used by the router's own `_buildRouteGuard()` ("no auth info -> fail open (setup/dev)"). Only an explicit `role === 'viewer'` hides it. Three enforcement layers, all client-side UX polish since the real boundary is the server 403: (1) the Send tab `<button>` gets the real `hidden` DOM attribute at render time for non-admins, not just a CSS class; (2) `_setTab('send')` itself refuses to switch for a non-admin, in case anything ever calls it directly; (3) the constructor's `storedTab` restore also re-checks admin status, so a viewer session sharing a browser with an earlier admin session (localStorage persisted `'send'` from before) falls back to `'packets'` instead of trusting the stale stored value.

**Verified with real (stubbed) V8-context execution, not just syntax checking**: 7 scenarios covering viewer/admin/no-identity/role-less-identity combinations for the constructor's `_isAdmin`/initial-tab logic, all passing exactly as expected including the "stale localStorage from an earlier admin session" edge case; a second direct check confirmed the actual rendered HTML has the real `hidden` attribute present for a viewer's Send button and absent for an admin's. `node --check` clean on both touched files (`app.js`, `dapnet_panel.js`); `tests/test_html_assets.py` 7/7; changelog bullet appended to the same-day Send-tab entry. **Not yet live-tested with a real viewer-role login** -- next step when picked back up.
